A compact magneto-optical trap has been successfully developed, using a planar-integrated design that merges an optical grating chip and a magnetic coil chip. This novel setup minimizes the size and weight of the trap, requiring only a single laser beam to capture a population of approximately 10,000 cold rubidium atoms. The improved MOT architecture has potential applications in devices such as gravimeters, atomic clocks, and quantum memory systems, offering a reduction in volume, weight, and complexity.

The spherically symmetric merging of a kinetic cloud of particles onto a Schwarzschild black hole is investigated. Unlike earlier research, which established boundary conditions at a distant point, we instead use an impinging gas cloud with infinite energy density, steady kinetic energy, and angular momentum. We demonstrate that this model corresponds to a more general, physically valid situation than previous studies, and that the impinging cloud can be represented by a series of decreasing radial power series. We use this new approach to investigate how a cloud with angular momentum affects the mass accretion rate and radiation force onto a black hole, and from there, derive a new series for the impact of these effects. Furthermore, we use our findings to compute modifications to the Schwarzschild metric and a new series for the change in a photon's radial energy, due to these effects. We also demonstrate that our impinging cloud model can be represented by a static, rotating black hole radius, which depends on the cloud's angular momentum and is less than the Schwarzschild radius. Finally, we use our impinging cloud model to establish a new series for the impact of these effects in a Newtonian black hole context, and compare it to a cloud with no angular momentum and infinite kinetic energy, which corresponds to the classic Painlev\'{e}-Laudat metric.

The probability of (de-)excitation and photon emission is evaluated for a non-relativistic, moving atom interacting with a quantum electromagnetic field near a stationary, perfectly conducting plane. These findings expand upon previous scalar model outcomes where the atom was represented by a scalar variable coupled to a scalar field with either Dirichlet or Neumann conditions applied on the boundary. This assessment considers how spontaneous emission rates change when an initially excited atom is accelerated versus an atom at rest encountering a moving mirror.

A longstanding issue regarding massive star origins involves whether these stars always form within dense clusters and, if found in less crowded environments, if they inevitably moved there.  Recent advances in wide-scale photometric surveys enable us to detect massive stars without bias in the less crowded regions of the galaxy.  This study examines forty candidate OB stars discovered by Mohr-Smith et al in the vicinity of Westerlund 2, with locations confined to a 1.5x1.5 degree square area, to determine if any share motion with the crowded Westerlund 2 star cluster.  Using Gaia DR2 astrometric data and spectra from Mohr-Smith et al, we obtain precise distance and motion estimates for these stars, indicating that six share motion with Westerlund 2, with some possibly being members of Westerlund 2 due to their transverse motion across the cluster, across a 30 million year timespan.  With none observed near the cluster's edge, this supports a flat density profile for massive stars.  This is the largest set of member candidates for Westerlund 2 and provides evidence that some massive stars can be found outside of dense cluster environments, with a density ten thousand times lower.  This implies that these stars must have escaped the cluster, with distended trails observed in Gaia data, suggesting that dynamical disruption is responsible for dispersing these stars, with further study required to understand how these stars originate and are ejected from their birthplace.

Degraded handwritten documents, which are susceptible to damage from paper ageing and environmental factors, can cause severe readability issues for current text recognition algorithms. To overcome these challenges, we propose an innovative, end-to-end approach utilizing Generative Adversarial Networks that not only restores visual clarity but also improves the overall readability of the documents. This pioneering method differs from conventional binarization techniques, which primarily focus on enhancing visual quality, by integrating a text recognition module to optimize generated output. The effectiveness of this architecture was validated through comprehensive experiments conducted on Arabic and Latin handwritten texts, showcasing improved readability and visual quality. Additionally, our pre-trained model demonstrated exceptional performance on the H-DIBCO challenges, even after fine-tuning on synthetic, degraded text images.

The growth of Information Technology has significantly altered how information is shared, making it necessary to convert printed documents into digital formats.  There has been an increase in fraudulent activities lately.  To prevent such account-related fraud, a system was devised which employs ID card extraction via OCR and NLP for verification purposes.  Optical Character Recognition, a technology that enables the conversion of images to text, can also be used to convert an Indonesian ID card or KTP into text format.  This facilitates easier data entry for service operators.  To enhance accuracy, the extracted text was further corrected using Natural Language Processing.  When tested using 50 Indonesian ID card images, the F-score achieved was 0.78, and the extraction process for each ID card took approximately 4510 milliseconds.

In vehicular communications, the complex and dispersive nature of channels makes reliable channel estimation vital for optimal system performance, yet the IEEE 802.11p standard's limited pilots lead to inadequate channel tracking. As a result, conventional IEEE 802.11p estimators experience significant performance decline, particularly in high-speed scenarios. To overcome these challenges, researchers have explored deep learning (DL) techniques for channel estimation in IEEE 802.11p. Nonetheless, these approaches either underperform in extremely high-speed situations or exhibit substantial computational complexities. To resolve these issues, this paper introduces an innovative solution based on a long short-term memory (LSTM) model for channel estimation. The proposed method incorporates an LSTM unit for channel estimation, followed by a temporal averaging technique to mitigate noise, and analytically calculates the noise mitigation ratio to verify its effectiveness. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed solution surpasses the performance of recently proposed DL-based estimators, while also achieving substantial reductions in computational complexity.

The task of automatically assigning colors to images without human involvement has garnered interest within the machine learning community for a limited time. Colorization is particularly challenging due to its inherently high degrees of freedom; when presented with an image, multiple plausible color combinations exist, and there may be no single definitive solution. Another related issue is Single Image Super Resolution, a task that involves converting low-resolution images into higher-resolution versions. This research targets a novel, end-to-end approach, called Progressive Color Shift Network (PCSN), designed to tackle colorization and improve the quality of low-resolution images by leveraging high-resolution images. The proposed network aims to learn color transformation between low-resolution and high-resolution image pairs, allowing it to enhance multiple versions of the same image with different colors. Notably, PCSN demonstrates superior performance on benchmark datasets for both the colorization and super resolution tasks, and its effectiveness is validated through a range of visual demonstrations and quantitative metrics.

We've developed a novel numerical scheme to efficiently calculate Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) weights without relying on tedious iterative processes. Based on the Universal Approximation Theorem, our proposed algorithm rapidly achieves low error rates in the regression and classification of intricate patterns, thus providing a practical approach to training ANN models. The algorithm's efficiency and adaptability are demonstrated through successful tests on various datasets, including the famous MNIST database for image recognition.

The ECFA Early Career Researcher's panel started representing the interests of young researchers within the ECFA community in January 2021. Throughout its first two years of operation, the panel developed its organizational framework, cooperated with ECFA by offering input and insights, and introduced several projects focused on comprehending and addressing the varied needs of young researchers. This report outlines the details of the panel's formation and operations as well as its engagement with numerous activities during its first two years of operation.

Confining modes at the edge, known as line waves, can propagate on the boundary between two specially designed electromagnetic interfaces that maintain mirror symmetry properties.
Studies have previously analyzed line waves in theory and in practice, revealing their occurrence at both microwave and terahertz frequencies.
It has also been demonstrated that these waves can occur when there's a sudden change from a negative to a positive symmetric resistance and uniform surface reactance present.
Characteristics of line waves include highly confineable mode propagation, polarization dependent on direction, and unique localized field enhancements.
A new study proposes a graphene patch structure, showing that the line waves produced can operate in the optical range.
The design involves a graphene surface integrated with an epsilon near zero substrate, which considers the effects of both dual and uniform reactive impedances.
However, this work specifically focuses on utilizing line waves in dual impedance structures.

One of the most effective approaches to building intelligent robotic systems is Learning from Demonstration (LfD), however research is still needed to overcome challenges such as multi-agent learning and prolonged autonomy.  A new architecture for multi-agent LfD is introduced which enables the creation of reliable and efficient robotic systems in complex and dynamic environments by leveraging advancements in Artificial Intelligence (AI) through the implementation of a Federated Learning (FL)-based collaborative learning environment involving both humans and robots. This novel approach capitalizes on local edge computing and AI-driven processes at multiple robotic platforms to generate a unified, AI-driven global model that is shared across the network, and utilizes human-robot interaction instances to inform learning. This innovative framework extends the traditional LfD approach to encompass multi-agent settings, incorporates human learning within existing robotic frameworks, and incorporates advanced AI methodologies to model interdependencies between robotic tasks, and it demonstrates its applicability through the implementation of a realistic industrial case study in a dynamic agile production system that recovers critical raw materials.

A new bias-corrected estimator has been created for the mean absolute deviation of a median regression model, addressing the problem of irregularity that typically hinders conventional bias reduction.  To overcome this limitation, a specific alternative strategy was implemented.  Establishing the bias correction involves verifying the local asymptotic normality property and a specific Bahadur-Kiefer representation.  Developed within the context of a traditional asymptotic framework, this proposal appears to retain effectiveness in high-dimensional settings, as evidenced by simulation results.

The tasks of relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction share a
common link in their objectives, allowing them to complement each other in the
process of predicting a subject-object relationship in a sentence. Specifically,
when a model identifies an object and its related subject, this relationship can
be utilized by the model to anticipate potential objects associated with the
subject, thereby enhancing the object's identification chances. Conversely, when
a model identifies an object and its related subject, this relationship can be
utilized by the model to anticipate the subject's related objects, thereby
enhancing the object's identification chances. Consequently, we have developed
a novel approach that integrates relation extraction and knowledge graph link
prediction called RE-KL, which surpasses individual performance by iteratively
refining each other's predictions. Our experimental findings demonstrate that
RE-KL achieves superior results compared to current standards in both tasks,
notably attaining a 5.44% improvement in the knowledge graph link prediction task
and a 3.25% improvement in the relation extraction task. Our full code and
dataset have been made publicly available.

The Analytical Exact Iteration Method has been employed to solve the N-dimensional, time-independent Schrödinger equation for complex-valued potentials, and further generalized to consider finite values of the quark mass. Calculations were carried out for N=2, 3 dimensions; and the binding energies of mesonic systems comprising J/Psi, Chi and Psi states were determined in the absence and presence of anisotropy. Anisotropy was found to raise the dissociation temperature for all quarkonium states except for the ground state in N=2 dimensions. Calculations were also made to verify the universality of thermodynamic properties derived from lattice QCD in the low-energy limit, and an approach to this limit was outlined.

Our study focused on the magnetic arrangements within the crystals of Tb3RuO7 and Nd3RuO7 using neutron-diffraction experiments. In Tb3RuO7, neighboring ruthenium atoms created a chain pattern, with some being ordered magnetically and others remaining randomly aligned. This unique combination resulted in an intermediate disordered state, with the two ruthenium types exhibiting similar yet distinct behaviors. In Nd3RuO7, the magnetic patterns were uniform and independent for the two ruthenium species, with both being ordered at temperatures below 17.5 K. We attribute the disordered state in Tb3RuO7 primarily to the magnetic frustrations, caused by the differing internal magnetic fields imposed by the ordered terbium atoms on the two ruthenium species, leading to distinct behaviors.

Multi-Layer Perceptrons are particularly effective at generating accurate
low-dimensional representations of data, such as images, shapes and light
fields. Despite advancements using periodic activations or positional
encodings, they have historically been tailored to process a single signal
component. In dual MLPs, two separate networks are combined to represent and
encode multiple signal variables. We enhance this approach by introducing a
novel dual-MLP architecture that integrates the synthesis and analysis
processes into a unified model. Through a series of experiments, our method
Demonstrates the benefits of using a dual-MLP approach for data representation
Obtains superior results on challenging 3D reconstruction tasks from single
images or video inputs. Provides significant performance enhancements over
existing state-of-the-art methods in video-based 3D shape reconstruction.

Traditional methods of covariate-shift adaptation utilize unlabelled data for either determining importance weights or domain-invariant features. Then, a model is trained using only labelled data. We're examining a special instance of covariate shift that also enables learning from unlabelled data, effectively merging adaptation with semi-supervised learning techniques. By drawing on causality concepts, we propose a novel method that requires learning from both the causes and effects of a target variable. This leads to the development of a semi-generative model, $P(Y,X_E|X_C,\theta)$, which is shown to be resilient against domain shifts in causal features. Moreover, this model leverages unlabelled data to directly map causes to their respective effects. Experiment results conducted on artificial data show considerable improvements in classification performance compared to solely-supervised and importance-weighting approaches.

Despite its impressive task execution capabilities, the inner workings of deep learning systems remain shrouded in theoretical uncertainty. In our study, we establish a geometric model for deep learning architectures by identifying connections to pre-existing geometric frameworks in quantum computation and diffeomorphic template matching. Within this context, we map the geometric structures of convolutional neural networks, residual networks, recursive neural networks, recurrent neural networks, and the equilibrium propagation framework. Furthermore, this geometric framework enables us to explore the relationships between geometric structures and the performance of different neural networks, thereby guiding the design of deep learning architectures at an algorithmic level.

We consider the field extension $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{d},\zeta_3)/\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_3)$ where $\zeta_3$ is a primitive cube root of unity and $d$ is a positive cube-free integer. Our work examines the behavior of the chain of lattice minima in the cubic field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{d})$ arising from the prime factorization of $d$ in relation to generators of ambiguous principal ideals. Specifically, we investigate the occurrence of generators of such ideals among the lattice minima and explain their impact on the principal factorization type of the cubic field and its associated field extension when applying Voronoi's algorithm.

A research framework is introduced to uncover and analyze decision-making processes from deep neural network classifiers in jet substructure tagging techniques. To achieve this, the study uses a novel method, incorporating 'augmented' variables, known as XAUG variables, alongside standard input, then applies a layer-by-layer relevance analysis to both types of networks. XAUG variables are merged with intermediate network layers and utilised in final stages to interpret the classification outcome. Analysis shows XAUG variables enhance discrimination capabilities when combined with low-level features, in some instances capturing the classification entirely. This method, combined with the relevance analysis, allows researchers to determine crucial information networks rely on and identify essential features. In the study's findings, incorporating XAUG variables in deep neural networks improved their performance by as much as 30-40\%, alongside presenting a novel method to quantify training uncertainty in deep neural networks.

For every positive integer r, a specific kind of Stirling number is used to count how many ways a set can be divided into a specified number of non-empty subsets, where each subset contains at least r elements. We're introducing a variation of these Stirling numbers, which represents their extreme forms, reducing to well-known cases when r equals one. This paper seeks to establish formulas linking these variations together.

Eighty sets of layer groups were examined, each consisting of four types: ordinary and double, as well as gray single and double. Layer group properties allowed for the efficient computation of relevant physical characteristics using symbolic methods, thanks to code such as POLSym. This involved an initial step of categorizing irreducible domains based on their action within the Brillouin zone and the topology of the torus. Additionally, band representations stemming from site symmetry groups were broken down into irreducible components. This theoretical data on layer group symmetry was then tabulated and made accessible online.

Momentum operators are explored in the context of intrinsically curved manifolds. It's established that for Killing vector fields representing these momentum operators, the manifolds are either flat or belong to specific categories: those with a compact structure and a constant sectional curvature of positive value, occurring in dimensions of 1, 3, or 7. Specific forms for these momentum operators and their associated Casimir element are studied, particularly for the three-dimensional sphere S^3. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the Lie algebra structure constants for S^3 relate proportionally to 2ℏ/R, where R represents the sphere's curvature radius, yielding countable energy and momentum spectrums for freely moving particles. A theoretical maximum for possible momenta in S^3 corresponds to its diameter, the de Broglie wavelength λ_R = πR. Building on this, the definitions and relationships for covariant position operators in terms of geodesic normal coordinates, along with commutator relations for position and momentum, are developed.

A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem.

In a composite Higgs model, where $SU(6)/Sp(6)$ is used, the flavor symmetry is identified as an $U(1)$ subgroup of $Sp(6)$. Here, the complex scalar field's', acting as a pseudo-Nambu-Goldstone boson, plays the role of a flavon, which bears a flavor charge. Upon the VEV of the flavon, $U(1)_F$ flavor symmetry is broken. This break results in the emergence of a small parameter and consequently generates a hierarchy between top and bottom quark masses. A flavon lighter than the TeV scale can naturally be introduced, which makes it a completely testable model to understand the flavor hierarchy origins. Furthermore, its effect on the substantial flavor-changing neutral currents arises and gets constrained heavily by flavor precision experiments. Research into the direct search for additional scalar bosons is conducted using HL-LHC and upcoming hadron colliders.

The use of Virtual-Physical Perceptual Manipulations, like redirected walking and haptics, extends VR interaction beyond conventional physical limitations by exploiting the boundaries of human perception, subtly guiding users' movements to enhance interactivity. This research examines the dangers of VPPM exploitation, beginning with a conceptual framework that confirms their existence and then applying speculative design to identify and mitigate threats. Through practical examples, we demonstrate how current VPPM practices can inadvertently create vulnerabilities that may lead to physical harm. This study seeks to highlight the potential consequences of VPPM applications and dissemination as they stand today.

To assess various approaches to expanding language coverage, we integrate German and Korean into BigScience's large-scale, 1.3 billion parameter multilingual language model, initially trained on 13 languages. Our study focuses on key factors influencing model adaptability for new languages and weighs the computational expense against potential performance gains.

Recent high-resolution observations using VLA and CARMA telescopes have unveiled previously unknown details of proto-stars in binary systems. Specifically, mass measurements for CB230 IRS1 and L1165-SMM1 revealed a significantly higher mass range ($0.1-0.25 \, M_{\odot}$) than those generally obtained from binary formation simulations, which were around $0.01 \, M_{\odot}$. In response to these disparities, researchers carried out numerical simulations of a core's collapse to analyze how a binary system's formation mass is influenced by its parent core's overall mass. In these simulations, they implemented azimuthally symmetric mass seeds within a rotating core, promoting the development of a dense filament, where a binary system might emerge. This binary formation process decreased as the core's mass increased, and it was generally observed that the binary mass was directly proportional to the core's magnetic to non-magnetic mass ratio. Furthermore, it was noticed that both systems CB230 IRS1 and L1165-SMM1 matched this predicted binary formation trend. In CB230 IRS1, researchers proposed that the lower-mass fragment in the system might develop into a brown dwarf, whereas in L1165-SMM1, they suggested that the higher-mass fragment could grow into a star with a mass up to $0.5 \, M_{\odot}$. These findings have given rise to two distinct binary formation theories, which might be different from each other and

This research introduces the m-arcsinh Kernel ('m-ar-K') Fast Independent Component Analysis ('FastICA') approach ('m-ar-K-FastICA') for feature extraction, combining kernel-based dimensionality reduction with ICA to overcome the limitations of previous methods. Although the kernel trick offers a powerful way to tackle non-linearity, its effectiveness can be undermined by a lack of open-source and reproducible kernel implementations, especially in complex datasets. The proposed m-ar-K-FastICA approach uses a readily available and adaptable Python library that facilitates collaboration with scikit-learn, providing a more reliable solution for feature extraction even in data sets with high entropy levels and no need for data pre-whitening. Several classification experiments using open-access datasets from diverse domains, including audio, medical, and text, demonstrate the capability of the proposed method to improve feature extraction and subsequent classification accuracy, particularly when data is highly non-Gaussian and non-linear. Furthermore, the computational efficiency of the proposed method makes it a viable option for applications with high data velocities, such as real-time processing.

This paper builds on existing research linking finite model theory to algebraic and propositional proof systems. It's demonstrated that if a logic system can identify unique, non-isomorphic graphs in a specific category, then a related proof system can do so as well, at roughly the same computational cost. This allows researchers to apply existing bounds from the latter system to the former, shedding new light on CPT's limitations. Establishing a polynomial CPT lower bound via a related PTIME-instance could resolve a long-standing question in finite model theory. Additionally, the findings provide a theoretical explanation for the separation between polynomial calculus and extended polynomial calculus within bounded-degree settings.

A subring collection in a ring $R$, that is associative, commutative nor unital, is defined as proper subrings set-theoretic union equating $R$. If such a collection exists, the ring covering number $\sigma(R)$ in $R$ is determined by the cardinality of a minimal collection, and a ring is $\sigma$ elementary when $\sigma(R) < \sigma(R/I)$ for any ideal of $R$, given it is non-zero, two sided and in $R$. The given text describes the discovery of first ring $\sigma$ elements that are non-commutative, and determines the ring covering number in $M_{2}(F)$, the ring of $2 \times 2$ matrices over a field $F$.

Social media platforms host an immense volume of content, encompassing a broad array of views on society. Despite the numerous opinions expressed, verifying their accuracy can be challenging due to their subjective nature. To address this, we aim to condense these posts into distinct narratives, thereby isolating the core assertions linked to specific topics. By gaining insight into and visualizing these narratives, social media debates can become more informed and productive. To establish a systematic approach for identifying underlying narratives, we propose PAPYER, a comprehensive dataset comprising online comments about public restroom hygiene, marked by an abundance of unfalsifiable claims. A collaborative human-AI pipeline is presented that uses a combination of machine and human intelligence to pinpoint the prevailing narratives, thereby outperforming existing large transformer models and unsupervised topic models.

Identifying trending social media events in real-time is crucial for various applications, such as monitoring elections, hurricanes, and protests. We have developed an approach using sparse signal processing techniques to accurately capture these movements on social media. Our method leverages multiple social media streams, each representing different topics or categories, and uses a sparse sensing technique to isolate significant changes as events unfold. We apply an l1, l2 heuristic, a greedy algorithm, and a sequential sensing technique to refine event detection, and have successfully tested our methods using real-world data from multiple sources. Our results demonstrate that these algorithms are not only effective but also adaptable, allowing them to detect events in various social media streams, such as Twitter and Reddit, and determine their corresponding volumes.

New, high-precision data from the cosmic microwave background lensing measurements and tomographic galaxy surveys in the upcoming years will enable researchers to make more accurate predictions about the properties of gravitational potential in the universe. By comparing these predictions with observations of galaxy clustering and galaxy-galaxy lensing, researchers will be able to assess the light's cross-sectional path and assess theories of gravity. We developed a weighted skew-spectrum based on the dark matter's matter-power spectrum and bispectrum, which can be used to analyze data from both galaxy clustering and galaxy-galaxy lensing measurements. We ran numerical simulations to study the skew-spectrum's effectiveness in quantifying the uncertainties associated with gravitational potential and non-Newtonian signal. Our results suggest that when analyzing galaxy clustering data, the skew-spectrum can effectively mitigate the impact of binary bias and tidal tensor bias, enabling researchers to make more accurate use of this statistic. We also discovered that galaxy-galaxy lensing data can be used to set limits on non-Newtonian signals, with specific limitations on tidal tensor bias parameters being more stringent than current constraints from galaxy clustering data. Our analysis reveals that when combining the results from both data sets, constraints on tidal tensor bias parameters can be more stringent, with limits potentially reaching up to $10^{-5}$, a value that is three times more stringent than current constraints.

By integrating Bayesian learning into adversarial training of deep neural networks, we developed a rigorous framework for training certifiable Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs). This approach combines constraint relaxation and modified cross-entropy loss to achieve robustness to potential attacks. The method, demonstrated through empirical tests on standard datasets, allows for training BNNs that are both accurate and certifiably secure on challenging datasets such as MNIST and CIFAR-10, further providing benefits in uncertainty calibration. This innovation facilitates the deployment of BNNs in applications requiring utmost reliability.

The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors about the virus. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its new adopters. Utilizing search frequency as a proxy for this metric, we identified many rumors that required attention from multiple fields, including public health, and developed a score to prioritize these rumors. Subsequent case studies confirmed the efficacy of our approach, revealing that many rumors scored high due to their alarming health-related content, whereas others scored lower despite being suspicious from the outset. Our research included an analysis of 154 rumors, influencing public perception with topics such as the pandemic's cause, treatment, transmission, and mortality rates. Our scores accurately ranked many of these rumors according to their perceived danger, even identifying a few that were later acknowledged as true but were considered particularly hazardous. Our study provided initial insights into the propagation of online rumors during a public health crisis, which could be used to develop and testing of effective countermeasures.

This study investigates the impact of hyperspectral pixel dimensionality reduction on classification tasks. Conventional image processing methods consider each pixel's spectral energy levels across the entire frequency spectrum, which often includes superfluous information that, when removed, doesn't alter the image's overall appearance. This study aims to determine the optimal reduction method by testing different techniques and evaluating their influence on pixel classification accuracy using a well-known dataset. The methods tested include straightforward dimensionality reduction, compression with a fixed rate, and adaptive rate with guidance from pixel classification information. A series of experiments were carried out to compare these techniques and measure their effectiveness. The findings suggest that compressing hyperspectral images by a factor of 50 to 100 times using a method independent of pixel classification yields relatively low loss in pixel classification accuracy, with images reduced by 75 times being the sweet spot before accuracy losses become noticeable. Moreover, the study discovered that class-specific compression methods can boost compression rates while minimizing accuracy losses, allowing for up to 90 times compression of accurate pixels while accurately classifying them. These findings suggest that hyperspectral images can be effectively compressed while preserving their classification accuracy, resulting in significant storage savings.

Neural networks are highly effective feature extractors but they pose significant challenges due to their large size. Understanding the parameters within various layers is complicated, resulting in the networks often being referred to as 'black boxes.' In contrast, simpler models are more interpretable but they are also much harder to find. Identifying and utilizing a sparse network that can be trained to replicate the same results raises questions, specifically regarding the existence of a smaller, trainable network that can match the performance of a larger, pre-trained network. This smaller network should be capable of training from the starting point, without relying on the original model's parameters. There are, however, concerns surrounding over-specialization when training these sparse networks and whether they can accurately represent the original model's features. This research investigates the existence of these trainable, sparse networks and explores their capabilities, while also probing the original model's representation and potential flaws. In the process, it discovers that the remaining, pruned parameters often serve as a form of regularization, preventing the network from over-fitting, even if the effects are negligible at times.

A novel prediction tool, referred to as ProCS, has been developed to forecast the chemical shifts of protein amide protons for proteins of any size and structure. Comparisons with other top-performing prediction software revealed that ProCS exceeded others in accuracy, specifically for proteins lacking a high-resolution structure. Furthermore, the utility of ProCS was demonstrated through predictions made on several enzymes. These predictions employed molecular dynamics simulations with a high-level quantum mechanics approach, leveraging multiple potential energy forces and refined water models. Data showed that predicted chemical shifts in confirmed regions of the protein could serve as a reliable reference for unconfirmed areas, ultimately contributing to a better overall structure.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant.

Describing the behaviors of complex systems comprised of strongly interacting elements requires concise expressions for their internal relationships. Ensuring the stability of these systems is the primary focus. Parquet theory is capable of achieving a level of self-consistency that encompasses all strictly pair-based interactions among elements. Grounded in a perturbative framework, the theory is comprised of a series of nonlinear integral equations that describe scattering events at all levels, constrained by principles of symmetry but also inherently heuristic. Within the context of a theoretical framework developed by Kraichnan, a new Hamiltonian-based analysis is applied to parquet's structure in the context of fermionic particles, resulting in a natural formation of the theory's underlying equations through its canonical representation. This approach reveals the inherent connection between the conserving properties of the derived scattering amplitude and the traditional parquet theory. Although the derived amplitude conserves properties at a microscopic level, it does not maintain symmetry. In contrast, the traditional amplitude maintains symmetry but fails to ensure conservation at any point. Ultimately, the decision to use one amplitude over the other is determined by the specific requirements of the system under consideration rather than its adherence to a theoretical ideal.

The process of exciton condensation leads to the spontaneous creation of electron-hole pairs and triggers a phase transition in a semimetal that forms an excitonic insulator by creating a gap at the Fermi surface. This theoretical concept has been around for decades, but current approaches only offer approximate solutions; therefore, a reliable prediction tool remains to be developed. To address this challenge, a new method was created that incorporates finite-temperature density functional theory and many-body perturbation theory to study exciton condensation. This method was successfully applied to two models: the hydrogen-like emtion gas and a semimetallic model, to predict the phase diagram of exciton condensation. The calculated results showed an agreement with analytical and exact-diagonalization calculations in all cases, thus demonstrating the accuracy of this new method. This approach is expected to be the most effective means of investigating exciton condensation in larger systems and predicting the critical temperatures for exciton insulators in real-world materials.

In the US, various safety organizations have adopted text-based systems for processing community members' incident reports, which necessitated a closer look at interactions between community members and dispatchers through these platforms. To investigate, researchers analyzed the system logs of LiveSafe, a community safety tool, combining quantitative and qualitative methods to identify patterns in the conversational flow. By developing a data framework that captured common incident-related information, researchers discovered dispatchers requested specific details from users, which varied based on incident types. Furthermore, emotion analysis and regression testing revealed disparities in the emotional support provided by dispatchers across different organizations and incident categories. Notably, dispatchers who showed emotional support received higher response rates and faster responses from users. These results have provided significant knowledge to practitioners and system designers, inspiring the development of AI-powered tools to enhance human service quality.

To analyze the impact of external magnetization on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with spin-triplet nematic superconductivity, we computationally investigate magnetic susceptibility in nematic and chiral superconducting states using the Ginzburg-Landau formalism near its critical temperature. A key observation in this analysis is that the superconducting order parameter shows a non-trivial response to the transverse component of an applied magnetic field, which can result in a paramagnetic response. Moreover, the topology of the Fermi surface exerts a substantial influence on magnetic susceptibility, with a specific Lifshitz transition inducing a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase and leading to the divergence of magnetic susceptibility at this transition point. Notably, the interplay between electron-electron interaction and competing phases of superconductivity is investigated, with results showing that the driving force behind a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase can be the presence of electron-electron interaction in the immediate vicinity of the transition. A comparison with existing experimental data is also presented in this analysis.

Label-efficient active learning algorithms query specific, representative samples to be annotated by a human. Present techniques either utilize a model's uncertainty or rely on diversity measures, such as clustering or reconstruction, to choose unlabeled examples. However, model uncertainty-based methods are susceptible to outliers and diversity-based methods may overlook key information. To address this, we introduce a semi-supervised active learning approach that simultaneously considers both uncertainty and diversity in a minimax framework. Our method incorporates a network that minimizes entropy and an entropy-maximizing classifier, while a discriminator is trained to distinguish labeled and unlabeled data. We then select the samples with the highest entropy that the discriminator identifies as unlabeled for human annotation. Experimental evaluation on image classification and semantic segmentation datasets demonstrates superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods.

To study how music changed over time from the year 1960 to 2010, we measured the
variety of songs in the Million Song Dataset using several elements, including
melodic complexity, rhythmic patterns, length, and tempo. By analyzing the popular
hits listed on the Billboard Hot 100 and randomly selected songs, we found that
most hit songs tend to be structured in simple ways, with the average complexity
score decreasing significantly over time. These results support the theory that
the most successful songs are those that listeners can easily recognize and remember
with their straightforward structures. Furthermore, we discovered that songs with
complex structures in relation to their keys are more likely to be considered classics
that last for a long time. By focusing on the relationships between the variables
that describe song variability, we used factorial analysis to create new variables
that capture significant patterns in the data. These new variables, obtained through
linear regression, revealed the key factors that influence a song's success, as well
as its genre and longevity. Finally, we mapped the relationships between these variables
using self-organizing maps to show how music has evolved over time from the year 1960
to the year 2010.

A novel category of stochastic processes that incorporate reinforcement involves sequences of random groupings denoted as $\{\mathcal{P}_t\}_{t \ge 1}$. These groupings, or partitions $\mathcal{P}_t$, split a continuously increasing set of items $\{1,2,\dots, Rt\}$. When time progresses to $t$, a fixed number of items $R$ are appended to this set; a fraction of these added items joins existing groups based on probabilities defined across different time intervals, initiating new subgroups separately from the ones that merged with existing groups. The items integrating existing groups make selections according to the group's current size proportionality, acting independently from each other. The items creating new subgroups, on the other hand, act independently and identically, producing subgroup configurations $\mathcal{S}_t$. The goal is to examine categories of stochastic processes that fit this description and related classifications, particularly $\mathcal{P}_t$ and $\mathcal{S}_t$, as they are both generated from the time-evolving groupings and have significant implications in random graph theory, genome evolution and macro-evolution, as well as the study of languages.
