This research received recognition through an award at the IEEE ICC 2021 conference.

The Natural Language Processing area has garnered disproportionate interest from researchers in the past. A primary factor driving this attention lies in the word prediction challenge, where given a sequence of words in a sentence, a model is tasked with recommending the subsequent word. Researchers have addressed this issue through various techniques, combining either syntactic or semantic analysis methods in the past. However, individually, these approaches often fail to yield practical results in real-world applications. For instance, latent semantic analysis can capture semantic text characteristics, yet it disregards syntactic constraints when generating word suggestions. In contrast, more advanced models like Deep Learning integrate both methods to achieve impressive outcomes. While these models can be computationally demanding, hindering their feasibility in certain scenarios, continuous advancements in technology and mathematical modeling enable the development of faster, more accurate systems. A hybrid word suggestion model proposed here, combining elements of Naive Bayes and latent semantic analysis, provides significant gains in both efficiency and accuracy, ultimately resulting in improved feasibility. Furthermore, the model's simplicity and adaptability for large datasets position it ideally for real-time applications.

Recent advancements in Session-based recommendation systems have gained popularity for providing personalized, real-time suggestions with high recall rates compared to conventional techniques. Recent examples include STAMP and NARM models, which, however, did not perform as expected on Zalando's Fashion-Similar dataset in comparison to a basic collaborative-filtering method. Our proposed strategy targets improving item ranking by leveraging the encoded session information through an attention network. Since both STAMP and NARM models are susceptible to ignoring session context due to focusing on individual items, we combine them using TF-IDF to incorporate context into the system, enhancing overall performance and item ranking accuracy. Our results indicate that the NARM component provides more beneficial context for recommendations compared to the STAMP model. After conducting extensive experiments on publicly available real-world datasets for both benchmarking and holistic session-based recommendation, we discovered significant improvements over NARM-only and a narm-stamp hybrid on various evaluation metrics. Our final model outperforms state-of-the-art baseline systems by showcasing greater recall and precision in top-n recommendation tasks, along with analysis of its key features and potential applications.

We examine a rigid structure composed of two active Brownian particles that interact in an activity gradient. We demonstrate analytically that the position of the dimer varies based on the angle between the particles and accumulates either at areas with high activity levels or low activity levels. This corresponds to chemotaxis and antichemotaxis respectively. Some dimer configurations display chemotactic and antichemotactic properties, with their behavior determined by the activity gradient strength. A coarsely detailed approach helps to generate an effective potential, used in our analysis to create a phase diagram. This diagram classifies dimer configurations based on their tactic behavior. This study provides valuable insights into the behavior of active colloidal dimers and informs the development of more complex systems composed of active nanoparticles.

A thorough approach is outlined to simulate single-phase flow in fractured porous media. The proposed methodology comprises three core components: generating an accurate 3D mesh of a fracture network, solving governing equations using a high-order numerical method, and implementing high-performance computing strategies. A mesh generation technique that handles problematic cases to maintain high mesh quality is provided. A versatile simulator utilizes process kernels to enable flexible interactions between the fracture and matrix domains. We validate the model through comparison with known analytical solutions and by examining numerical convergence in different scenarios. Two case studies are presented: the first investigates how fractures can impact flow in different configurations, and the second explores flow and transport through a large stochastically generated network of 257 fractures.

This study centers on low-energy collision avoidance strategies for autonomous drone swarms. Two key approaches, optimal control and differential flatness, are more typically utilized for a single vehicle. However, these methods are adapted to work seamlessly together for multiple vehicles in this research. Numerical simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed differential flatness method in reducing energy consumption while successfully avoiding collisions. Compared to the optimal control method, the differential flatness technique has the advantage of being easier to implement and requires less computational power.

This research explores various spectral characteristics of the Seidel matrix associated with a connected chain graph, demonstrating that $-1$ is always an eigenvalue, while other eigenvalues may have a multiplicity of at most two. We derive the multiplicity of the eigenvalue $-1$, the minimum number of unique eigenvalues, eigenvalue limits, the characteristic polynomial, and bounds for the Seidel energy of a chain graph, which outperform previously proposed energy bounds by Haemers. We also obtain the minimum Seidel energy for specific chain graphs of order $n$, along with presenting several unresolved questions.

In our investigation, we focus on a mean-field optimal control issue for stochastic differential equations featuring time-delay, which are influenced by fractional Brownian motion with a Hurst parameter exceeding 0.5. Given the fractional Brownian motion's nature, which defies the criteria for being a Markov process, we resort to the fractional White noise calculus and specialized tools for differentiating functions of measures to establish necessary and sufficient stochastic maximum principles. This approach is further exemplified by two applications, including solving a delayed consumption optimization problem from a cash flow and a linear-quadratic problem under delay constraints.

We've developed a unique, detailed two-parameter set of finite-band Jacobi elliptic potentials that correspond to the non-self-adjoint Dirac operator, seamlessly linking two well-known limit cases, each associated with the absence or presence of elliptic parameters. To thoroughly analyze the Dirac operator's spectrum, we've made connections between periodic/antiperiodic eigenvalue problems for the operator, equivalent tridiagonal operator actions in weighted Hilbert spaces and relevant Heun equation connection issues. This, in turn, ties into four related non-self-adjoint, unbounded tridiagonal operator eigenvalue problems which surprisingly possess real eigenvalues.

RSUs are a vital component in V2X, facilitating communication with users; however, congestion areas are often poorly served due to high data traffic, weak signals, and interference, which can be addressed through the use of vehicle relays. To enhance the network in these situations, this research utilizes stochastic geometry to develop an innovative analytical framework for the performance evaluation of vehicular networks incorporating RSUs, vehicle relays, and mobile vehicle users. Our two-dimensional analytical model effectively considers the spatial interdependence of RSUs, vehicle relays, vehicle users, and road infrastructure using a Cox point process. By assuming relay backhaul to RSUs over reserved wireless channels and user association with the closest RSU or relay, we calculate the probability that a typical user is linked to either an RSU or a relay, determine the SIR coverage probability of a typical user, and subsequently, calculate the average effective transmission rate of a typical user within the network. This method enables the quantification of the increase in average effective transmission rate resulting from the deployment of relays.

Wikipedia's ultimate goal is to be an authoritative reference on various topics.  However, due to a limited number of editors and a vast amount of articles, only 0.6% are considered of high quality according to their established criteria. To enhance article quality through machine learning, we must first label individual sentences as high or low quality, yet this process relies on human annotations that are time-consuming and often yield inaccuracies. To resolve this, we developed an automated system that examines semantic modifications in Wikipedia edits to create labels, considering the pre-edit version as an example requiring improvement, and high-quality sentences as instances that need no improvement. By employing our labels in machine learning models, we found that performance improves over relying on existing, manually generated labels. Furthermore, we discovered that Wikipedia editors' behavior provides more accurate labels compared to crowdworkers who lack the same level of contextual understanding and agreement as editors.

Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. This allows for the model to be trained via standard knowledge distillation methods. When access to the original data isn't possible, pseudo-samples are created based on the network's decision boundaries and assigned soft labels, which serve as a transfer set for training the model. Our proposed approach is evaluated on multiple networks and datasets and shows positive results. Code is available at: https://github.com/zwang84/zsdb3kd.

Researchers have observed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decay mode for the first time, and have also gathered evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decay mode, utilizing a 3.0 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ dataset of $pp$ collisions collected at 7 and 8 TeV center-of-mass energies by the LHCb. The branching fractions for these decays are calculated as follows: The $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 \bar{K}^0_S$ branching fraction is estimated at (4.3±0.5±0.3±0.3±0.6) ×10^-4, and the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} \bar{K}^0_S$ branching fraction is estimated at (2.8±1.0±0.3±0.2±0.4) ×10^-4, with the given uncertainties stemming from various sources.

The $C^*$-algebra formalism of topological T-duality developed by Mathai and Rosenberg is applied to a broad class of topological spaces encompassing torus bundles, nilmanifolds, and other examples from string theory. By constructing T-duals from commutative $C^*$-algebras with ${\mathbb R}^n$ action, we establish a simple method for achieving this transformation. Our work rigorously addresses almost abelian solvmanifolds across arbitrary dimensions, offering clear group-theoretic criteria for classifying classical T-duals and providing explicit, continuous-trace algebra computations for the resulting non-trivial Dixmier-Douady classes. Ultimately, we demonstrate that any solvmanifold can be represented as a $C^*$-algebra bundle of noncommutative tori, which we explicitly compute, while the monodromy of the original torus bundle is translated into a Morita equivalence among fiber algebras.

Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, confirming the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external supervision.

This paper proposes a metric function that yields an optimal performance on average, which significantly reduces decoding computations while maintaining superior error-correction performance for polarization-adjusted convolutional codes. With our proposed metric, the PAC code decoding computations are merely 2% of the original function decoding computations, achieving better error-correction performance and significantly reduced decoding computations.

This project tackles the complex problem of simultaneously monitoring the positions and shapes of hands and objects in a sequence of depth point cloud data, starting from the known poses in the initial frame. To achieve this, we introduce a network called HandTrackNet, the first point cloud-based hand joint tracking system, to calculate hand joint movement between frames. Our novel hand pose canonicalization module simplifies this task and enables accurate tracking of hand joints. By converting these joints into a template-based hand model called MANO, our system can reconstruct the entire hand. To track objects, we use a module that generates object SDF data from the first frame and performs optimization-based tracking. Then, we run a NewTon dynamics system on the optimized joint angles to predict the future pose. In order to resolve the partial observable issue of NewTon dynamics, we employ a layer that predicts the object pose directly. Our system can be trained end-to-end by combining the hand and object trackers with NewTon dynamics. Experimental results demonstrate the (1) state-of-the-art performance of our hand tracker compared to the best existing hand tracker; (2) significant improvement in our full system when compared to independent hand and object trackers; (3) success of our partial object tracker prediction; and (4) benefits of incorporating our NewTon dynamics system over existing tracking methods.

This study employs the modular reduction technique to a Coxeter group of rank 4 featuring a star diagram with 5, 3, and k= 3, 4, 5, or 6 labels, using the odd primes from the ring Z[tau], where tau represents the golden ratio. It categorizes each reduced group as a reflection group over a finite field and demonstrates that the reduced group retains its properties regardless of the used prime in the reduction process.

A novel, markerless extrinsic calibration system is introduced that relies on real-world depth camera data rather than simulation or fiducial markers. Our system leverages machine learning to automatically develop and utilize real-world models for identifying and positioning the end-effector, predicting object rotation, and pinpointing critical points in a single image. A mathematical transformation and a keypoint-matching algorithm allow us to accurately estimate end-effector pose based on rotation and keypoint data. Enhanced system robustness is achieved through a combination of advanced algorithms, including the iterative closest point method, multi-frame processing, filtering, and outlier detection. Results show our method's calibration and pose estimation capabilities can be as precise as sub-centimeters and sub-degrees with minimal and unseen test poses; we have also found that incorporating data from just one optimal pose yields comparable accuracy.

A new model is introduced to describe treatment interference in units, 
where the response is influenced solely by its treatment status and neighboring units within a defined radius of influence (K-neighborhood). Traditional approaches for identifying interference involve controlled randomized trials and statistical tests focused on specific, selected units - the so-called focus units. We provide criteria to select focus units that minimize the risk of false positives resulting from unobserved interference beyond the chosen radius of influence. In simulations, the proposed methods outperform existing methods, and these are further validated through two real-world studies, one in paint adhesion and the other in music preference.

Calculations of neutrino emissions from self-destructing dark matter particles within a star are being conducted. In the core of a star that has not yet undergone nuclear reactions, it's observed that the interactions between these particles and the star's constituent atoms via a particular particle can produce an unusually high number of neutrinos, which may equal and potentially surpass those produced by the star's nuclear reactions early on. This process primarily involves two reactions: a collision of two dark matter particles resulting in neutrinos or intermediate particles that then decay into neutrinos, which may be confined to less than 1-2 percent of the star's volume and persist throughout the star's lifetime. This information is then used to assess potential impacts of this process on the cooling of a star in the context of existing constraints on dark matter particles.

The ongoing UNIONS project, the most comprehensive optical survey to date in the Northern sky, has partnered with CFIS for $r$-band data collection, boasting exceptional seeing of 0.65 arcseconds and complete magnitude 24.5 for precise science applications. With two overlapping fields, specifically with COSMOS and ECDFS, we have tapped into a wealth of ground-based and space-based data, including photometric redshifts for 350,000 galaxies and 200,000 with multiple observations. By applying a two-dimensional shear calibration technique to 80,000 galaxies, we have successfully removed residual multiplicative bias and confirmed zero additive bias. With multiple bands at our disposal, we have calculated the Hubble constant using multiple methods, one of which yields a value of $H_0=73.1\pm 3.2$ km/s/Mpc. Additionally, we have constructed a massive bulge-dominant galaxy sample and used it to determine the total stellar mass of the COSMOS field, achieving exceptional accuracy by applying shear calibration to mitigate size biases. With a total of 62,000 photometrically-selected late-type galaxies at our disposal, we have analyzed their correlation function, discovering that there is no significant deviation from the Planck consensus at large scales but a notable discrepancy at smaller scales. By applying a volume-occupied bias correction, the projected mass density and redshift-halo model are aligned, revealing an unexpected ascendancy in the mass occupancy of

A notable consequence of a finding made by Veech more than 50 years ago, relating to the mod $2$ form of the Kronecker-Weyl theorem, has to do with sequences of irrational rotations of the form $\{q\alpha\}$. In the event that a certain number $\alpha$ resists being closely approximated by rational numbers and another number $b$ in the interval $(0,1)$ differs from the rotation sequence for no integer $c$, then, as $q$ grows larger, the sequence of sets $\{0\leq x<b\leq q\alpha\}$, where the lower bound $x$ takes on all natural numbers, exhibits evenly distributed parity for the number of elements in these sets for almost every value of $\alpha$ as well as $b$. A prior study by Bishop and Damian made a related discovery with respect to the behavior of certain triangular arrays. Our research presents an interpretation of their findings within the context of a specific domain of irrational rotations, which is particularly similar to an earlier finding by Veech, albeit with additional restrictions. Our work seeks to explain this connection between their work and ours.

We prove that for k-rational singularities of local complete intersections, k-Du Bois classification applies. For hypersurfaces, k-rationality can be determined based on the minimal exponent. Moreover, certain local vanishing properties for k-rational and k-Du Bois singularities have been identified. These properties were also discovered separately by [FL2].

We've observed the appearance of field-induced Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless correlations in a weakly coupled, spin-1/2 Heisenberg material called [Cu(pz)2(2-HOpy)2](PF6)2. Due to its moderate exchange coupling of about 6.8 Kelvin, the application of laboratory magnetic fields produces a noticeable anisotropy of the spin correlations in an XY plane. This significant BKT regime develops because of a weak interlayer exchange of about one millikelvin that causes 3D correlations as the critical temperature is approached, resulting in an exponential increase in spin-correlation length. Nuclear magnetic resonance, muon spin resonance, and neutron scattering experiments are used to study this phenomenon in (Cu(pz)2(2-HOpy)2)(PF6)2.

Adding three right-handed neutrinos and a simple QCD axion sector to the Standard Model effectively explains multiple phenomena including neutrino oscillations, dark matter, and baryon asymmetry. In doing so, it also resolves issues with strong CP problems and stabilizes the electroweak vacuum while fitting within observational limits of Higgs inflation. The model, referred to as $a\nu$MSM, generates dark matter through the diffusion freeze-out of axion-like particles or through the mechanism of dark sterile neutrinos, with an appropriate choice of parameters able to explain both neutrino oscillations and dark matter in a consistent manner.

This study optimizes the execution time of established algorithms for classically simulating quantum circuits comprising Clifford and T gates. The efficiency improvement stems from deriving a novel upper limit for the number of stabilizer states required to express $m$ copies of the magic state, $|T\rangle$. The findings reveal that a superposition of no more than $O(2^{\alpha m})$ stabilizer states can accurately represent $|T\rangle^{\otimes m}$, where $\alpha\leq 0.3963$, surpassing the previous best-known estimate of $\alpha\leq 0.463$. This advancement allows for the development of a classical algorithm capable of approximating the output probabilities of $n$-qubit Clifford + T circuits $U$ within a specified inverse polynomial error margin, using a time complexity of $\mathrm{poly}(n,m)2^{\alpha m}$. Furthermore, the investigation also yields refined bounds on the stabilizer rank of symmetric product states $|\psi\rangle^{\otimes m}$, ultimately leading to the creation of a strong simulation algorithm for circuits comprising Clifford gates and multiple instances of a fixed single-qubit Z-rotation gate, operating at a time complexity of $\text{poly}(n,m) 2^{m}$, an improvement over prior work.

This research employs the Tsallis holographic dark energy model in two scenarios, 
non-interacting and interacting, to calculate essential parameters for the energy 
density equation of state within the FRW universe, analogous to a quintessence model.
We will reassess complex quintessence by modifying its potential and analyzing 
scalar field dynamics, followed by evaluating the differences in and stability 
of two scenarios, namely non-interacting and interacting.
We will examine the plausibility of these scenarios as real universe descriptions 
by calculating the fractional energy density, $\Omega_{D}$, and analyzing two parts 
of the quintessence field effect: the complex and real parts. We assume the real part 
behaves as a slow-roll field.
We understand that scenarios with a fractional energy density ($\Omega_{D} > 1$) do not 
accurately depict real universes. Furthermore, we introduce an interacting coupling 
parameter, $b^{2}$, linked to the Tsallis model's constant parameter ($\delta$) with 
respect to a fractional energy density ($0.73$).
Notably, unlike real quintessence, we identify an interdependence between the fractional 
energy density, interacting coupling, and other parameters in this theory.
Ultimately, we visually illustrate and compare ($\omega_{eff} - \omega_{D}$) relations 
for both non-interacting and interacting scenarios, distinguishing them from the standard 
quintessence model behavior.

Between October 2019 and April 2020, the LAMOST performed a unique observational study using four $K$2 plates. This study, which involved low- and medium-resolution spectroscopic surveys, gathered a significant amount of data. The low-resolution spectroscopic survey yielded around 767,000 spectra after 25 nights of 46.6 hours of exposures and a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 for about 70% of its spectra. The medium-resolution spectroscopic survey took 177 exposures and around 49.1 hours over 27 nights to collect around 478,000 spectra. The data showed a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 for about 50% of its spectra. To estimate the stellar parameters and radial velocities, the LAMOST research team utilized several different methods such as LASP, DD-Payne, and SLAM. These estimations demonstrated good agreement and were consistent with those of the APOGEE study. By analyzing the $Gaia$ DR2 data, the LAMOST research team corrected for radial velocity zero points on a per exposure basis, showing good alignment with the APOGEE study. To estimate stellar masses, the LAMOST research team utilized stellar parameters and multi-band magnitudes in combination with distances and extinction values. Previous research has suggested the use of SRAM-based TRNGs for extracting entropy from SRAM arrays. As these arrays are commonly employed in specialized or general-purpose chips for data storage, SRAM-based TRNGs provide an economical alternative to dedicated hardware TRNGs. Nevertheless, existing SRAM-based TRNGs suffer from reduced throughput, elevated energy expenditure, prolonged latency, and a limitation to generating random numbers continuously. In order to overcome these shortcomings, this paper presents an SRAM-based TRNG that can sustain long periods of operation. To accomplish this goal, we introduce a novel approach, termed TuRaN, which utilizes a lower supply voltage than recommended to cause SRAM access failures, then applies the SHA-256 hash function to these faults to create high-throughput random numbers. We validate the practicality of TuRaN through SPICE simulations on diverse process nodes and assess its reliability through real-world experiments conducted on two commercial FPGA boards. Furthermore, we demonstrate the high quality of the random numbers produced by TuRaN using the NIST standard randomness tests and note its exceptional performance with respect to throughput, energy consumption, and latency.

A preliminary design and simulation of a single-electron resistive switch has been developed, incorporating two linear molecules that interact electrostatically: one molecule is a single-electron transistor and the other is a single-electron trap. To confirm our design's validity, a theoretical analysis was performed, integrating ab-initio electronic structure calculations with a general single-electron tunneling theory. The outcomes demonstrate that these tiny molecular constructs can process electrical signals at extremely high speeds while also storing information over extended periods and exhibiting a substantial ratio between active and inactive current levels. Additionally, simulations have shown that self-organized monolayers built from these molecules could also function as resistive switches with comparable properties and the capacity to withstand flaws and irregularities in electrical charges.

The concept of loop-tree duality has emerged as a promising approach for numerically computing complex multi-loop scattering amplitudes, offering an attractive alternative to conventional methods. By applying loop-tree duality, the Feynman integrands are simplified to a form that only captures physical information, resulting in a causal representation. In this discussion, we explore the application of all-loop causal representation to describe multi-loop Feynman integrands, which can be characterized by loop topological features and connections. To address numerical evaluation, we consider two methods based on the relevance of individual loops, either including or excluding a particular loop from the integral. By examining the residual integral after omitting a loop, we can derive an equation that relates the original integral to a modified version with reduced complexity. Through systematic application of these principles, we can break down complex multi-loop amplitudes into a series of simpler, loop-by-loop corrections, facilitating numerical computation. To validate our approach, we have successfully computed the numerical values of certain two-loop double-resonance Feynman integrands, which match the results obtained via other methods.

This paper aims to provide a direct and straightforward proof of a specific eigenfunction expansion formula for one-dimensional quantum walks with two possible states, similar to analogous work done on Sturm-Liouville operators by renowned mathematicians. A related theory involving the CMV matrix already addressed this topic, yet our approach is unique as it focuses specifically on the mentioned quantum walks and also yields valuable properties of Green functions. These properties enable us to derive a precise formula for a positive-matrix-valued measure, ultimately allowing for a direct computation of the spectral measure in a particular model known as the two-phase model.

This study examines the composition of hybrid stars formed by neutrons, protons, and various other particles. The analysis combines the Sigma-omega-rho model for a specific nuclear phase with two distinct quark phase models, and incorporates Maxwell and Gibbs conditions to understand the phase transition. By analyzing mass-radius relations, a hybrid star's mass is predicted to be limited to twice the mass of the sun.

The introduction of $q$-deformation into optomechanical systems reveals opportunities to amplify non-traditional optical phenomena. This insight drives an investigation of the optical behavior within a linearly coupled $q$-deformed optomechanical system. Composed of two deformed cavities interacting with mechanical mirrors and coupled through a network, this study reveals that $q$-deformation enhances the speed and magnitude of phase transitions during optical windows. Furthermore, we find that for specific $q$ values, fourth-order systems can exhibit rare optical transparency, explaining this through the behavior of coupled $q$-deformed oscillators. Ultimately, we determine that $q$-deformation accelerates the transition between optomechanical ground and rare optical states.

In a previous study, I developed a model where the Two-Rotors Model's negative scissors states, consisting of two-sided classical bodies, exhibited 1 |K| = 1; 0 components and negative space parity. Building on this work, I explored reflections in a plane that aligns with the rotors' symmetry axes, resulting in R-negative states with positive parity. Furthermore, I established a connection between reflections and R-operations, relating them to specific internal changes within the rotors, which I then used to calculate and compare the electromagnetic transition strengths of these states with those of their positive scissors mode counterparts.

The properties of thin films made from metallic transition-metal oxides show significantly different behavior compared to their bulk counterparts. A comprehensive study is conducted to investigate thin films of LaAlO$_3$ and SrTiO$_3$ with varying thicknesses, grown by the epitaxial growth method on substrates made of transition-metal oxides. This study aims to examine the unique phenomenon known as charge ordering, which occurs in thin films of these materials when they are at least a few nanometers thick, and are typically insulating in nature. Through the analysis of thickness-dependent resistivity measurements, it is discovered that charge ordering does not take place in the thickest films investigated, which are several nanometers thick. Instead, these films remain insulating due to the presence of disorder caused by discrepancies in lattice mismatch with the substrate, and are found to exhibit tunable insulating to metallic transitions through the adjustment of oxygen pressure. A model combining disorder and electron interaction is used to explain these observations, which reveals that the thickness-dependent transition from insulating to metallic behavior is consistent with the dilute 2D Hubbard model.

The occurrence of diffusion can be seen across various natural phenomena, and this widespread application is attributed to the broad implications of the central limit theorem. In the past, scientists discovered an extension of typical dynamics, resulting in "anomalous" diffusion that accounts for distributions characterized by long, power-law tails. One such physical system - laser-cooled atomic ensembles - offers an optimal platform to study such phenomena, primarily due to its distinctive friction force. This interplay between laser cooling and anomalous dynamics is thought to be a groundbreaking area of research, and our latest experiment investigates the effects of stationary forces within these systems. By performing numerical simulations based on the Smoluchowski equation, scientists have studied the effects of different forces on the system's behavior. These simulations have provided precise predictions that were experimentally verified, and our findings have demonstrated the accuracy of the predicted power-law tails under specific conditions. This research has successfully bridged the theoretical and experimental domains, and our results have contributed significantly to understanding anomalous dynamics, while also uncovering new aspects of laser-cooling phenomena.

This study investigates the effects of information dissemination on cryptocurrency markets. Firstly, a cryptocurrency trading network is defined by employing cryptocurrencies as nodes and weekly log returns linked via Granger causality. The analysis traces its development over time, focusing on years 2020 and 2021. The logarithmic US dollar price returns of this network are then examined using Granger causality and O-information to quantify both pairwise and high-order statistical relationships. The Granger causality results indicate that most cryptocurrency networks exhibit asymmetric information flow, with oscillations often being predictive. Notably, the Granger causality hypothesis is challenged by a significant number of rejections, suggesting the presence of hidden variables. Furthermore, a more comprehensive high-order statistical analysis using O-information reveals the critical role of stable coins in the cryptocurrency network, as their returns significantly predict other cryptocurrencies. The Granger causality results for weekly returns are consistent with those found in daily research, but the significance of rejections is relatively lower. Consequently, the logarithmic US dollar price returns of the 2020 cryptocurrency network are predicted by a multivariate linear model that incorporates the effects of information dissemination.

The formation of particles from trace gases is a crucial source of cloud condensation nuclei that facilitate the creation of clouds due to their role in overcoming extremely high supersaturated conditions needed for homogeneous water droplet formation. The application of quantum chemistry in modeling this process has improved significantly due to its enhanced precision and efficiency in calculating the configuration of particles. Nonetheless, even advanced approaches continue to rely on the classical nature of nuclei, which is uncertain for certain systems. The current research evaluates the influence of zero-point motion in the simulation of small clusters of sulphuric acid and water using path integral molecular dynamics at the density functional theory level. Generally, the incorporation of zero-point motion results in the distortion of the mean particle structure, promoting greater proton transfer compared to classical behavior. The incorporation of zero-point motion in the simulation is found to expand the accessible range of proton positions between a sulphuric acid and water molecule at a given energy level. The incorporation of zero-point motion in the simulation is found to expand the accessible range of proton positions between a sulphuric acid and water molecule at a given energy level, which is also reflected in the simulated pairwise bond lengths. The incorporation of zero-point motion results in a more uniform electron density between the molecules, which facilitates the formation of hydrogen bonds at a supersaturated water-junction, whereas classical simulations fail to replicate this phenomenon at a supersaturated water-junction, whereas classical simulations fail to replicate this phenomenon.

We establish the definitions for a compact perception pair, understood as a totally bounded measurement space coupled with a proximal relation, as well as for a compact approximation fixed point subset. It's proven that any metric space with a compact perception pair possesses at least one point that serves as a fixed point for all closural mappings. Furthermore, it's been demonstrated that the space of continuous functions on a compact domain is not only complete with the sup metric, but also has a compact perception pair, thereby guaranteeing the existence of a fixed point for all closural mappings in this space. In contrast, the space of continuous functions on a compact domain does not possess a compact approximation fixed point subset.

The way solids respond to temperature gradients can be understood by likening it to gravity's effect in space. In studying this, researchers investigate whether this analogy accurately describes the collective behavior of quantum Hall states and other chiral topological systems. By analyzing the Haldane model, which simulates different environmental conditions, they examine the consequences of two scenarios: one with variable gravity and electrostatic forces, and another with variable temperature and chemical potential resulting from interactions with surrounding electrons and phonons. The study reveals that this thermal analogy does not hold; while an uneven gravitational force induces specific energy flows, a comparable uneven temperature has little to no effect in systems that exchange energy with their surroundings weakly. Additionally, the similarity between an external electric charge and the system's internal energy potential is also invalid under these circumstances.

In various machine learning scenarios, simpler models are generally preferred to their more complex counterparts, and controlling model complexity is a major objective for several methods, such as regularization, hyperparameter optimization, and architecture planning. For deep learning models, understanding how complexity is controlled has been a challenging task, given that many conventional methods are unsuitable for their inherent complexity. Our research introduces a concept called geometric complexity, quantifying the variability of model functions using a discrete Dirichlet energy metric. By combining theoretical analysis with empirical evidence, we demonstrate that several widespread training heuristics, such as parameter and spectral regularization, as well as parameter initialization techniques, serve to control geometric complexity.

A new approach for directly extracting the Wilson coefficients of rare $b\to s$ processes is developed using $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays within an unbinned maximum likelihood framework. This novel method outperforms traditional Wilson coefficient determination by utilizing all available data and accounting for experimental correlations without segmentation into $q^2$ bins. Simulation results confirm the improved sensitivity and potential to leverage the complete Run 1 and 2 LHCb dataset in practice.

Automated essay grading has been a persistent challenge in Natural Language Processing.  Despite years of research, it remains an only partially resolved issue, with notable practical applications and research implications.  Techniques such as transfer learning and data augmentation have significantly improved the accuracy of state-of-the-art models in this domain.  Past research has explored the potential of Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and variants like Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), among others, in solving automated essay grading.  Our study focuses on the development of a state-of-the-art automated essay grading model using cutting-edge transformer-based architectures like BERT and RoBERTa, in conjunction with data augmentation methods.  We thoroughly evaluated our approach on multiple datasets, analyzing various factors that influenced performance, and achieved superior results, surpassing the current state-of-the-art in performance on four distinct datasets.

Given a simplicial complex defining a tensor's marginalizations, we restrict them to rank one, an idea developed from Kirkup and Sullivant's work on toric models. We delve into the toric ideals arising from these marginal independence models, and demonstrate that for each model, there exists a linear transformation that converts its toric ideal into a more general, polynomial ideal representing the marginalizations, often not expressible linearly.

A higher education system or similar opportunities can drive social mobility across generations by allowing individuals to rise above their family's economic status. To understand the extent to which this social mobility occurs, a new index was created to measure the ability of societies to move up the economic ladder. The index, which has a maximum value of 10, considers three key factors: access to higher education opportunities, the ability to pass wealth down to the next generation, and median wealth levels. When compared to other developed nations, the US sits in the middle of the social mobility pack, between Sweden and Norway at 9.50 out of 10.

The symmetry of wavefunctions under parity for particles of arbitrary spin is responsible for determining the wavefunction exchange statistics when the particles are permuted. According to non-relativistic quantum mechanics, the properties of angular momentum alone account for the sign factor resulting from the particle permutation, which relates spin to particle exchange statistics in this context.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
The Delegated RingCT scheme is comprised of an integrated signature and encryption framework, combining a public key encryption protocol and two types of signatures along with linkable ring signatures, alongside non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs.
A comprehensive description of Delegated RingCT, along with security evidence and an implemented prototype, are presented, which we subsequently test through benchmarking analysis.
While Delegated RingCT may not possess the same level of anonymity compared to other RingCT implementations, we propose that its ability to be compatible with DPoS consensus mechanisms provides a reasonable trade-off for enabling a more efficient and scalable decentralised cryptocurrency with preserved anonymity capabilities.

If more specific subclasses of linear systems can be solved in near-logarithmic space, this capability can be applied to solve a broader range of linear systems within a similar space complexity. Our findings build on work by Kyng and Zhang who previously made similar discoveries in terms of time complexity, utilizing reductions between approximate solvers; our own proof demonstrates that these reductions can be implemented using threshold circuits with specific characteristics.

Researchers have made the initial detection of three massive gauge bosons simultaneously produced in high-energy collisions between protons.  These collisions were performed at the CERN LHC with the CMS experiment's data set that contains 137 fb$^{-1}$ worth of information.  Separate searches were conducted for various combinations of bosons, including W boson variations, and have found no significant anomalies in the data, only sticking closely to standard model predictions.  The researchers have set new limits on possible non-standard model processes involving multiple boson production, including one scenario where three bosons are produced with an significance of 3.2 standard deviations beyond background expectations.

Previous foundational Hebrew NLP tasks have heavily relied on the 30-year-old Hebrew Treebank. This outdated single-source corpus lacks the diversity of modern Hebrew, found primarily on the web. This research paper addresses this issue by presenting a new, open-access UD Hebrew treebank. This corpus, created by sampling various topics from Hebrew Wikipedia, provides a much-needed upgrade to NLP's understanding of contemporary Hebrew. The project evaluates its own annotations, validates results using automated tools, and achieves new state-of-the-art results on UD NLP tasks by combining advanced language models with innovative approaches. The project's samples, annotations, and data, as well as its source code, are freely accessible on GitHub.

It is proven that for each $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$ and $x_1,\ldots,x_n \in L_p(\mu)$ where the largest absolute value among them does not exceed $K$, there exists a vector $y = (y_1,\ldots,y_n) \in \ell_p^m$ with dimension $m = \log^2 (3n/\varepsilon)$, such that the inequality $\mu \left( \big\{ i : x_i^p \ge \varepsilon \sum_{j=1}^n x_j^p \big\} \right) < \varepsilon$ holds and the difference between the maximum and norm of $y$ is less than or equal to $2 \sqrt{\ln(4/\varepsilon)} K y_1$. Recent breakthroughs in artificial neural networks have accelerated the growth of data-driven modeling in mechanics, making cooperative modeling more feasible. As research advances, diverse teams can create new models and data, leading to shared knowledge and collaboration opportunities. Nevertheless, a challenge persists in neural networks' tendency to 'forget' previous tasks after training on new ones. This drawback restricts cooperative learning, since adjusting an existing model to address a new problem can negatively affect performance on earlier tasks handled by other teams. To address this issue, the authors developed a groundbreaking 'continual learning' method and successfully implemented it in solid mechanics for the first time. They utilized recurrent neural networks to predict the behavior of materials undergoing plasticity. Notably, the developed method can be adapted for use in a range of network architectures and to predict multiple phenomena. This study's purpose is to stimulate innovative applications of continual learning, facilitating collaborative strategies among the mechanics community in addressing increasingly complex problems. Results demonstrate that the employed method can enable sequential learning of multiple constitutive laws without memory loss and often with reduced data requirements, matching or exceeding the accuracy achieved through standard training of separate models for each law.

Current studies examining the performance of randomly assembled low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes usually assume the independence of degree distributions from edge endpoints. In contrast, our research extends this understanding by investigating LDPC ensembles that incorporate degree-degree correlations. We propose novel techniques for generating degree-degree correlated LDPC ensembles, derive density evolution equations applicable to binary erasure channels, and employ numerical simulations to illustrate how degree-degree correlations impact LDPC code performance. Interestingly, our findings indicate that negative degree-degree correlations can enhance the maximum error tolerance of LDPC codes, with further increases potentially yielding superior unequal error protection designs.

An advanced modular system, which is known as the safety filter (SF), has been heavily utilized in controlling nonlinear dynamic systems to enhance performance and ensure safety. The system consists of an element that predicts and filters disturbances: the predictive safety filter (PSF). In this paper, the PSF is greatly improved by incorporating an estimation correction module. This improvement significantly boosts the accuracy of the disturbance estimation process. The corrected disturbance estimation is then used in two distinct control strategies: the minimum control effort and robustness-based filters. The proposed system's effectiveness is validated through simulation experiments in various challenging scenarios, showcasing its ability to surpass the traditional MPSF performance in both safety and performance aspects. The improved system is also capable of achieving significant safety and performance enhancements even when the system is subject to significant errors in the disturbance estimation process. The proposed system's performance is compared with the traditional MPSF, with experiment results demonstrating its ability to achieve major safety and performance enhancements, even when the disturbance estimation process is inaccurate, which is a significant error for MPSF. The overall system's effectiveness is evaluated through simulation experiments in various challenging scenarios, showcasing its ability to surpass the traditional MPSF performance in both safety and performance aspects.

A critical flaw in the security of quantum key distribution (QKD) stems from device imperfections that can be exploited by adversaries through side channels. We have developed a novel approach that enables the detection of these imperfections without the need for reliable device parameters. In our experiment, a customized source of entanglement, which mimics real-world device limitations, was used to generate Bell-state correlations. We found that this correlation was subject to a non-uniform distribution, with a non-convex shape. As a result, the classical simulation hypothesis, which is a fundamental principle in QKD, can no longer be applied. We have further demonstrated that this non-uniformity can be leveraged by adversaries to break the security of QKD. In order to mitigate this issue, the post-processing phase in the QKD protocol can be modified to handle the non-uniform distribution. However, this mitigation comes at the cost of reducing the key rates. In our study, we explored the trade-off between security and key rates under various scenarios.

Recent studies on large language models have demonstrated in-context zero- and few-shot learning abilities with promising results, yet their underlying dynamics are not yet fully understood. For instance, there is limited knowledge about how learning in-context changes when using varying training corpora. Our research aims to explore the influence of a pretraining corpus's origin and size on the performance of a Korean-centric model. Notably, we discovered four crucial findings: Firstly, a pretraining corpus's domain significantly affects the model's ability to learn in-context. Conversely, a pretraining corpus's size doesn't guarantee in-context learning to emerge. Furthermore, a pretraining corpus composed of multiple domains may facilitate the development of in-context learning. Lastly, a pretraining corpus of non-domain specific content might be insufficient for in-context learning to take place. These results imply that a pretraining corpus is a critical component in developing a model with in-context learning abilities and selecting an appropriate one is essential.

Galaxy cluster observations have primarily focused on the formation of central nebulae, yet little is known about what happens when the initial, intricate structure of these formations disintegrates. To investigate the long-term effects of this process, we conducted 30 million test simulations to study the development of cold gas clouds under various physical conditions within a galaxy cluster. Our research indicates that in the initial stages, these clouds maintain their complexity, however, as they pass through shocks, they break apart into simpler, cloud-like formations that can persist for millions of years. These clouds, known as "stranded fragments," have minimal kinetic energy, yet, due to their small size, they eventually dissolve at a relatively low threshold in terms of thermal energy. However, if a cluster possesses abundant, cooling gas, these fragments can survive, act as barriers, and influence the behavior of filaments, as well as, on rare occasions, give rise to secondary, central nebulae through cooling processes. Our findings indicate that in the majority of cases, cold gas fragments dissolve, but in the event that a cluster is surrounded by a halo, these fragments can survive for an extended period of time, up to 20 million years. This implies that in the event that a galaxy cluster interacts with a halo, it is possible for the evolution of cold gas to extend beyond 20% of the cluster's virialization phase.

The examination of $C\!P$ violation in beauty- and charm-hadron decays serves as
a crucial test of the Standard Model's predictions, also acting as a sensitive
indicator to uncover physical phenomena not accounted for within the SM. The
presentation includes precise measurements of observables connected to the
unitary triangles stemming from unitarity constraints on the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-
Maskawa matrix describing quark mixing, alongside recent $C\!P$ violation
measurements in beauty- and charm-hadrons. Specific emphasis is given to an
analysis that initially identified $C\!P$ violation in beauty baryons and made
the most accurate measurement of this effect within the charm system to date. 
These analyses rely on data gathered from proton-proton collisions in 2011 and
2012, collected by the ATLAS, CMS, and LHCb experiments.

New high-energy string interactions have been discovered in 10D open superstring theory. These amplitudes have unique polarization properties and their counterparts in bosonic string theory are significantly weaker. A remarkable relationship exists among these amplitudes, where one is proportional to the others. Calculations of their ratios confirm a long-standing theory prediction made by Gross in 1988. Additionally, the total count of newly calculated high-energy amplitudes in superstring theory is consistent with those from recently discovered fermion interactions in string theory.

To effectively manage the vast amounts of data being generated by a growing number of mobile and IoT devices, future mobile networks (MNs) must shift from traditional resource allocation methods. By integrating computation capabilities into Base Stations, we can optimize resource usage and efficiently manage resources near the edge. Leveraging techniques such as time-series forecasting and control theory, we propose using neural networks and optimizing strategies within the Multi-access Edge Computing paradigm. Our approach involves online algorithms for virtualized resource scaling, reconfiguring computing and communication assets, and enabling dynamic BS switching to minimize energy consumption and ensure Quality of Service (QoS). Numerical results demonstrate that these strategies lead to significant reductions in MN energy consumption, with up to a 50% decrease in some scenarios.

The objective of zero-speech synthesis is to create a vocabulary-independent speech system without transcription data, requiring the transformation of training data into acoustic units for test synthesis. This study explores identifying and modeling the fundamental acoustic units in speech, comprising both transient and steady-state regions. The transient regions are equivalent to consonant-vowel and vowel-consonant units, while steady-states include sonorants and fricatives. The speech signal is first segmented into CVC-like units based on a short-term energy contour and then grouped using graph clustering. The clustered units are initialized to include transient onset and decays, and steady-state rhyme components, and are subsequently rearranged into acoustic units in an HMM-GMM framework. The AU sequences are then used to develop synthesis models, and the effectiveness of the approach is demonstrated through the analysis of subjective and objective scores on the Zerospeech 2019 challenge database. The results show that acceptable quality speech synthesis at a low bit rate can be achieved.

Optimizing multi-limbed robots' motion under posture and force constraints poses a challenging nonlinear optimization issue, often accompanied by extensive computation times. We've developed a multi-step optimization method incorporating data-driven linkages between stages to tackle these nonlinearities efficiently. Both cluster analysis and evolutionary strategies are applied to determine the specific parameters of McCormick envelope relaxations, allowing us to leverage learned constraints across preceding stages, thus yielding better performance, faster solution times, and more interpretable outcomes. Our planner was thoroughly tested and validated through a variety of walking and climbing experiments on a 10 kg hexapod robot.

We have developed two overarching methods to quantify the manipulation of quantum states using probabilistic protocols constrained by specific quantum resource limitations.
Initially, we formulated a fundamental criterion for achieving a physical transformation between quantum states using a previously introduced resource metric.
This approach led to the discovery that the metric is not only necessary, but also sufficient, for one-shot resource conversion in various resource theories, effectively rendering more restrictive protocols unnecessary.
By employing this metric, we were able to refine the performance limits of one-shot and multi-copy probabilistic resource distillation protocols.
Concurrently, we introduced a comprehensive technique for calculating achievable probabilities in resource transformations through a series of convex optimisation problems.
This approach enabled us to precisely assess the trade-offs between probabilities and errors in the distillation of maximally resource-rich states.
Furthermore, we successfully demonstrated the efficacy of our methods in the analysis of quantum entanglement distillation.

We investigated the dynamic behavior of a cup of coffee being carried while in motion, by applying a lumped model that combines characteristics of a planar nonlinear pendulum. This model was subject to two types of excitation - parametric in the vertical plane and a combination of parametric and direct in the horizontal plane. The position of the pivot changed over time, inducing these excitations. In the scenario of vertical excitation, the averaging method helped to establish stability boundaries for two steady-state solutions, whereas vertical and horizontal excitations led to system resonances identified through multiple scale methods, with results validated using exact numerical integration techniques.

In our research paper, we address the challenge of a regularized distributionally robust learning problem in decentralized networks by taking into account the changes in data distribution. By incorporating the Kullback-Liebler penalty into the robust min-max optimization framework, we transform the problem into an efficiently solvable form and propose a robust decentralized optimization method, specifically DR-DSGD, based on the Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD). Under specific conditions and a sufficiently large regularization parameter, we analytically prove that our algorithm achieves a rate of convergence of $\mathcal{O}\left(1/\sqrt{KT} + K/T\right)$. Furthermore, experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of DR-DSGD, yielding an improvement of up to $10\%$ in test accuracy over various data distributions. DR-DSGD exhibits greater communication efficiency, with reduced communication rounds by up to $20$, compared to traditional DSGD, while also ensuring fairness across decentralized devices.

We utilize the concept of hydrodynamic attractors to establish a universal relationship between initial energy states and the number of produced particles in high-energy collisions. By combining this with an in-depth model of energy release, our findings demonstrate that entropy generated before equilibrium is established naturally accounts for the common trend of decreasing particle production with increasing centrality observed in nucleus-nucleus collisions. Additionally, we calculate the energy density of the initial state and outline potential avenues to utilize our research to determine non-equilibrium characteristics of the quark-gluon plasma.

Using complex simulations of star-forming clouds, the process by which powerful jets form is studied under different magnetic field strengths and mass accumulation rates. The data show that strongly magnetized clouds produce fast-moving jets only when the protostar gains a relatively small amount of mass per year, typically no more than 10 to the minus 3 solar masses. However, this low-mass rate also means that less-strong magnetic fields are required to produce the high-velocity jets. For very high mass accumulation rates, the high-velocity jets appear initially, but quickly weaken and then disappear completely, which makes it impossible for these low-velocity outflows to form early in the protostar formation process, especially in magnetic clouds that are very weak, leading to different star formation processes than what is typically observed.

This study investigates the optimal equilibrium between performance capabilities and operational limitations for a specific category of nonlinear systems, encompassing balanced command filtered backstepping (BCFB) and balanced performance control (BPC). A novel approach involves introducing a performance safety assessment (PSA) metric that measures system safety in the presence of instability-inducing conditions, specifically known as the beta parameter (\boldsymbol{\beta}). This assessment enables continuous monitoring of the system's ability to maintain performance and detect potential threats to stability. This ongoing assessment is utilized to develop a modified BPC strategy, incorporating safety-critical information to mitigate the system's tendency towards instability. This enhanced BPC is further combined with filtered backstepping (FB) to form the basis of a safety-oriented control system. Ultimately, numerical simulations are employed to demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in maintaining and improving system performance while detecting and mitigating potential stability risks.

This research project seeks to offer fresh perspectives on how various gravitational interactions affect an object orbiting the Earth. Primarily, it explores the impact of the Earth's shape and other bodies on the object's trajectory. Specifically, the project examines how the Earth's oblateness affects certain orbital configurations and identifies how the object's area-to-mass ratio influences its interaction with the second degree gravitational effects. To provide practical applications, the project aims to establish how the object's area-to-mass ratio impacts the accuracy of models representing its orbital behavior. Ultimately, the project aims to contribute to our understanding of how the Earth's gravitational field affects small bodies.

We examine the techniques of simulating light-matter interactions within tight-binding models that derive from first-principle theory. The conventional method for describing optical properties uses a velocity-based approach tied to the vector potential. An alternative method exists, where a finite system is represented through the electric field, resulting in a dipole-based model inspired by Peierls substitution. This study evaluates the accuracy of both methods in relation to gauge invariance, utilizing TB models constructed from maximally localized Wannier functions and applied to two-dimensional paradigm materials. We calculate the electromagnetic responses under linear and strong excitations, comparing the outcomes to converged first-principle simulations to validate our TB models' accuracy. The results indicate that the dipole-based model yields a more precise description than the velocity-based model. We attribute this to the imperfect compensation of diamagnetic and paramagnetic currents in the velocity-based model. To rectify this shortcoming, we formulated a sum rule that explicitly addresses the compensation issue, allowing the correction of velocity-based models to match dipole-based models and guarantee gauge invariance.

In a problem focused on category-level perception, we consider utilizing sensor data to identify and understand objects within specific categories despite variations within those categories. An active shape model, where pre-defined CAD models of various objects are used as a reference, is employed to determine the 3D pose and shape of an object. Our first achievement is developing PACE3D* and PACE2D*, which are novel optimisation algorithms ensuring accurate results for both 3D and 2D keypoint data, through the use of precise mathematical formulations. Additionally, we have developed versions of these algorithms robust to outlier data, labelled PACE3D# and PACE2D#, with a framework called ROBIN for identifying and pruning these errors by utilising a graph theory method to identify compatible data sets. Our research also includes thorough testing with various simulated datasets and a real-world PASCAL dataset, where PACE3D# has demonstrated success in outperforming existing solutions on vehicle detection and has application in real-time.

We will define a confidence area for parameter estimates of a sample of size $N$ derived from random variables following a Cauchy distribution. By considering the Cauchy distribution's parameters as a single complex parameter, combining location $\mu$ and scale $\sigma$ as $\gamma = \mu + i\sigma$, we will determine a region within the complex plane, ultimately defining it as both a disc and a square using a straightforward formula.

A new statistical method is developed for basket trials to assess the effectiveness of a new treatment in multiple patient subgroups under one protocol. This approach uses Bayesian statistics to optimize sample size and allows information sharing between groups. We develop formulas to ensure each subgroup trial meets specified criteria, comparing the new treatment to a control, by clinically relevant standards. For subgroups with pre-defined similarities, we find the minimum required trial sizes simultaneously. Our approach resembles frequentist methods when there's no sharing of data. Notably, by allowing data borrowing, we find smaller trial sizes needed than traditional methods that don't share information. We illustrate the effectiveness of our approach using two actual trials. Further simulations demonstrate our approach maintains accuracy in detecting positive results without increasing false positives.

To satisfy the rising demands of high-throughput in the industry, advanced motion systems must now be designed with a delicate balance between high-speed and high-accuracy. However, conventional control strategies often struggle to meet these requirements, particularly in motion systems that are susceptible to changes based on their position. This research introduces a cutting-edge modification to traditional control designs to address the performance limitations in these systems, effectively allowing for improved motion control even under dynamic conditions. The effectiveness of this innovative approach is showcased through simulation-based testing in two distinct scenarios involving linear motion systems, resulting in significant velocity and accuracy enhancements while maintaining precise motion control.

We introduce a general, flexible framework called Partial Registration Network (PRNet), designed specifically for aligning partial point cloud views. Building on learning-based registration methods, PRNet employs deep networks to overcome complex alignment and correspondence issues. Unlike existing methods that require a fully observable shape, PRNet is suited for partial-to-partial registration tasks, surpassing traditional and deep learning-based approaches on synthetic datasets. Our approach features self-supervised learning of a suitable geometric representation, a keypoint detector for common point identification, and a general network that combines various learning methods for registration. Experimental results demonstrate PRNet's ability to consistently predict keypoints and correspondence across different views, while maintaining geometric similarity across datasets.

A group G is said to have property $R_\infty$ if all automorphisms $\varphi$ of G make the number of twisted conjugacy classes in $G/\ker\varphi$ finite. In this paper, we determine the finite nilpotent groups that possess the $R_\infty$ property.

Instead of presuming hypothetical new physics will be found at future colliders, 
we consider a different possibility where there isn't any. In this case of 
predictive physics, the focus shifts to thoroughly understanding the electroweak 
sector and making precise predictions about quantum corrections for precision 
tests. To achieve this, the focus is on the stability of the Higgs potential and 
the predictions about the top quark mass, based on the standard model defined at 
$\mathcal{O}(100\,\mathrm{TeV})$. This involves choosing a natural cutoff for the 
standard model and making a choice about its naturalness. A choice is made to 
maximize the naturalness of the model by selecting the smallest cutoff. This 
cutoff can be compared to the planck scale, providing an estimate of the 
naturalness. Furthermore, the necessary precision for quantifying naturalness 
is calculated, considering future measurements of the top quark mass that could 
be achieved with a high-luminosity $e^+e^-$ collider. This study examines the 
bounds on the fine-structure constant and the mass of the Higgs boson that would 
result from requiring the standard model to be a low-energy description of nature 
up to the TeV threshold.

A new technique is developed to process time-sensitive data from ultra-fast experiments using an approach based on optimization in a pathway framework. This technique is successfully tested on data from experiments involving X-ray scattering and electron diffraction to analyze the breakdown of molecules. Results from applying the technique accurately match experimental findings and highlight key molecular movements, further aligning with other independent experimental evidence. What's more, this approach effectively considers the continuity of molecular structures and is resilient against noisy data.

We present the results of the first calculations of the longitudinal and transverse light-front distribution amplitudes for several mesons, specifically $D^*$, $D^*_s$, $\rho$, $\phi$, $K^*$, and $J/\Psi$. This calculation also yields distribution amplitudes for the vector kaon, providing confirmation of lattice QCD predictions; in contrast to expectations, we find a nearly symmetric longitudinal distribution and an obliquely shaped transverse one, indicating a substantial contribution to momentum from the strange quark.

We investigate key properties of several types of Gelfand-Shilov spaces, which are characterized by the decay of their smooth functions and their Fourier transforms. The nontriviality of these spaces, specifically ${\Sigma}^{\sigma}_s$, is shown to depend on the values of $s$ and ${\sigma}$ being greater than 1. The text further presents growth estimates for functions within one-parameter spaces, and it also establishes relationships between short-time Fourier transforms and these spaces. Moreover, conditions are established to ensure that Toeplitz operators are continuous when applied to functions within one-parameter spaces.

Segmentation of unseen imaging modalities without manual labels presents significant difficulties due to the considerable time and resources needed for annotation. Current techniques typically address a novel modality either by fine-tuning a pre-trained model or by dividing the tasks into independent image translation and segmentation steps. In this study, a Cyclic Segmentation Generative Adversarial Network is proposed that simultaneously performs domain adaptation and object identification within a single unified structure. Apart from standard CycleGAN losses and supervisory signals from labeled domains, additional self-supervised objectives focusing on object-relation masks and object features are employed to enhance the generator's performance. Evaluations on the segmentation of neuronal nuclei using EM images and unlabeled ExM images confirm that the proposed CySGAN outperforms previous techniques in terms of boundary sharpness and overall quality.

Our proposed algorithm, Feature Mapping RNN, leverages key concepts in machine
learning, including parameter sharing, Radial Basis Function kernels, and
adversarial training, to develop a novel RNN architecture for generating future
video features and anticipating actions. By using only the initial video frames and
a reduced number of parameters, Feature Mapping RNN efficiently generates future
features, which are then used in a multi-layer perceptron equipped with an RBF
kernel layer to accurately forecast actions. In our experiments, Feature Mapping RNN
achieved superior performance on JHMDB-21, UCF101-24, and UT-Interaction datasets
compared to existing state-of-the-art models.

Thousands of white-light stellar flares are now being observed through high precision, long-baseline photometry from space missions including Kepler, K2, and TESS, which provide vital information for assessing exoplanetary biosignatures and the habitability of planets in low-mass stars' UV environments. Despite this advancement, a critical limitation remains in evaluating these variables, which stems from the lack of data on near-ultraviolet spectral stellar flares. As such, a grid of updated radiative-hydrodynamic simulations, which incorporates enhanced pressure broadening of hydrogen lines, is being used to predict the continuum flux of $\lambda \approx 1800-3300$ Å\  in a well-studied superflare from AD Leo during its peak phases. This prediction model utilizes semi-empirical combinations of radiative electron beam flux spectra and atmospheric heating rates, which are based on observations from solar flares, combining both theoretical and empirical elements. When compared to existing models, our findings indicate that existing models significantly underestimate the continuum flux, particularly in the near-UV range, which could influence photometric searches for biosignatures on exoplanets in low-mass stars with high energy flares.

We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. A one-to-one connection exists between nearly parallel G2 structures and real Killing spinors, enabling the deformation theory to be formulated through the use of spinors and Dirac operators. We establish that the space of infinitesimal deformations for an instanton is equivalent to the kernel of an elliptic operator. With this approach, we prove that abelian instantons exhibit rigidity, and subsequently apply these results to define the deformation space of the canonical connection on nearly G2-manifolds with a normal homogeneous structure of four dimensions.

A bounded linear operator $T$ on a complex Hilbert space with a countable basis is referred to as C-normal if it satisfies a particular condition under the action of a conjugation operation. Specifically, $T$ can be said to be C-normal if there exists a conjugation operation $C$ on $H$ such that $TC^\ast CT = C^\ast T^\ast T$. In the context of function mappings, a self-map $\varphi$ of the open unit disc can be described using a linear fractional expression. This work investigates the conditions under which the composition operator $C_\varphi$ and weighted composition operator $W_{\psi, \varphi}$, where $\psi$ is another function, are both C-normal operators for specific conjugation operations $C$ and $\psi$.

This paper delves into a type of partition that excludes elements divisible by p. Specifically, the study targets p-core p'-partitions which adhere to these constraints. Notably, the largest of these p-core p'-partitions can be modeled by a long walk through a p-vertex graph, with edges assigned via the modulo p addition rule. Moreover, the research also identifies a systematic collection of significant p-core p'-partitions that establish a substantial lower limit on their maximum size.

Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for these models against deceptive transformation-based attacks. Initially, we classify frequent three-dimensional transformations into three types: shearable (such as stretching), compositional (such as rotating), and indirectly compositional (such as skewing) transformations, then we use these categories to develop general formulas for translating these transformations into translation-based point clouds, from which we obtain a proof of concept for a general formula that translates any shearable transformation. This concept involves embedding the original point cloud, along with an auxiliary line, into a new point cloud through a sequence of simple translations. We demonstrate the feasibility and precision of this framework in practical scenarios such as PCL using a specific example of a spinning transformation. Additionally, we propose a reliable method called SOT to robustly protect these point cloud models. By integrating the framework into the training process of the neural network-based point cloud model, we achieve robustness against various manipulation attempts. Our experiments confirm that the inserted line has minimal impact on the point cloud and demonstrate the superiority of our solution in handling transformation-based attacks.

We're investigating medium access techniques in Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar networks with all radar units utilizing identical settings, such as sweep duration and frequency characteristics.
