We're developing and evaluating ALOHA and CSMA protocols to minimize the impact of narrowband interference, introducing a new metric to gauge performance based on network throughput. In the case of ALOHA, we analyze the probabilities of interference and system efficiency under different system parameters. We observe that FMCW network behavior diverges from typical wireless communication patterns. In some scenarios, increased packet transmission can decrease interference probabilities. We introduce a clear channel assessment process, known as medium sensing, for CSMA, also defining metrics to gauge its effectiveness. In our analysis of CSMA, radar units transmit data after confirming an empty transmission path. We examine CSMA's medium sensing success rate, interference probabilities, and system efficiency under different system parameters. Unlike standard communication networks, the optimal strategy in some scenarios may involve the highest feasible attempt rates for maximizing throughput. Extensive simulations are conducted to validate our analytical findings and compare the efficiency of slotted ALOHA and CSMA. In our analysis, CSMA consistently outperforms ALOHA across all practical use cases.

Recent experiments employing various methods have sought to detect the entangled two-photon absorption phenomenon across a range of materials. A new investigation adopts a distinct approach, focusing on analyzing changes in a Hong-Ou-Mandel interferogram resulting from entangled photon interaction. Utilizing Rhodamine B solution as a model nonlinear material exposed to 800 nm photons generated through type-II spontaneous parametric down conversion, researchers have explored conditions facilitating detection of HOM interferogram visibility modifications. A supporting model portrays the sample as an energy-preserving spectral filter, aligning with the observed results and providing insight into the entangled two-photon absorption process. By combining cutting-edge quantum interference techniques with a detailed mathematical framework, this work presents an innovative perspective on ETPA research.

We calculate rational T-equivariant elliptic cohomology of complex projective spaces derived from finite dimensional T-representations V. This is accomplished by establishing that the T-equivariant elliptic cohomology theory constructed by Goresky and MacPherson is equivalent to the Goresky-MacPherson theory's restriction on T-representations V. As a direct result, we find the rational T-equivariant elliptic cohomology of CP(V) expresses the sum of the T-equivariant elliptic cohomology of complex lines with dimensions matching the irreducible, finite-dimensional T-representations V.

Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a leading approach for
inferring accurate and missing event and temporal knowledge graph information.
Building upon successful applications of tensor decomposition in static graph
completions, we introduce Time-LowFER - an extension of the low-rank factorization
model that is both efficient in parameters and attentive to time constraints.
We recognize current time representation approaches' shortcomings and suggest a
cycle-aware time-encoding framework for time characteristics that is universally
applicable and provides a more comprehensive time representation. Our unified
framework focuses on processing time-sensitive data within temporal knowledge graph
embeddings and demonstrates the benefits through our experimental results on two
notable benchmark datasets.

In the field of rigid-body impact sound synthesis, the sound produced by the ground is often overlooked. However, in this study, an idealized ground sound model, rooted in elastodynamic theory, is used to determine under which conditions ground sound is perceivable, rather than being masked by the sound produced by the impacting object or its transient vibrations. An analytical model derived from this theory allows for the calculation of the acceleration of the ground surface in a precise and mathematically closed form, which can then be applied in various simulation methods to generate the sound waves. It is found that ground sound can be audible under certain circumstances when the sound produced by the impacting object is inaudible, specifically when a heavy object strikes a soft surface and when the point of impact is positioned at a shallow angle relative to the listener's location.

A prevalent form of demonstrating Bell nonlocality known as the all-versus-nothing proof is presented without the use of inequalities. This concept consists of two main species, referred to as "always-type" and "sometimes-type", which have received significant research attention. Past studies on "always-type" all-versus-nothing proofs have primarily involved perfect correlations from stabilizer states. This has led many researchers to conclude that perfect correlations are the sole means of yielding "always-type" all-versus-nothing proofs. Contrary to this prevailing notion, our study offers a "always-type" all-versus-nothing proof rooted in non-perfect correlations. This research aims to clarify an enduring misconception and potentially expands our understanding of Bell nonlocality while also opening avenues for advancements in quantum information technologies.

In flat band systems, constrained environments result in unique properties tied to the minimal eigenstates, which exhibit complete randomness in variational space. This randomness limits the effectiveness of designing artificial flat band systems, as even small-scale protocols face a substantial challenge. A newer approach involves flat band generation using higher-dimensional surfaces and the study of flat bands on 2D lattice walls as models for 1D systems. However, artifical creation of these systems in the many-body scalar product space faces a problem of finding a path that maps a given state's scalar product with a maximally random eigenstate to a flat band eigenstate. A new algorithm addresses this issue by leveraging the gradient descent method to optimize this space. This innovative approach expands the scope for designing flat band systems, enabling the development of more complex, multi-component protocols. A key aspect is the minimalization of artificial Hamiltonian's expectation value under the constraint that the system remains in a flat band. This has been successfully demonstrated in a simple numerical example consisting of a three-component artificial flat band system formed based on the scalar product space of a specific quantum spin model's many-body states.

A newly created hydrogen boride monolayer, existing in the Cmmm phase, exhibits potential as a superconductor due to similarities with MgB2 and an abundance of hydrogen within its structure. Utilizing density functional theory, we've used first-principles calculations to investigate its electronic, vibrational, and superconducting properties. Contrary to expectations, however, the hydrogen boride system fails to possess a notable superconducting critical temperature. Hydrogen in this compound impairs the bonding between boron atoms, thereby reducing the effectiveness of electron-phonon interaction. Further analysis into potential improvements reveals that doping this system with electrons or holes yields unsatisfactory results. Consequently, the critical temperature of this superconductor cannot be significantly elevated through these methods.

Research on the division of quantities into equal parts continues to evolve. The findings presented here coincidentally relate to the numbers A124324 in the Online Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences. A distinct counting method is developed for these numbers, and we establish a one-to-one correspondence between a specific type of division and the division of quantities into fewer equal parts. Furthermore, we introduce a set of numbers, $f_{n, k}$, which represent the count of a specific type of division containing $k$ distinct segments. Recursive relationships defining these numbers, along with their differential generating function, are provided. Identifying a closed form expression for these numbers is a desirable outcome. Lastly, we generalize our results to scenarios where the first segment consists of different parts, accompanied by combinatorial evidence.

We categorize and understand a certain aspect of attractiveness in groups that use arithmetic, and derive statements indicating a dual nature related to their stable components, characteristics, patterns, and associated algebraic structures. To accomplish this, we study the movement patterns over the characteristics of the part of these groups that are stable and have manageable properties, particularly demonstrating the rigidity where any stable movement remains unchanged, which is a more comprehensive interpretation of Furstenberg's earlier work concerning patterns on the torus. Additionally, under the assumption that the group has a certain higher-level structure, we prove that the movement patterns over the characteristics of these groups that are stable and have manageable properties, and have a certain complexity structure, exhibit rigidity as well.

Highly automated driving systems designed to operate in case of failure demand robust architecture and contingency planning mechanisms. To safeguard against electric and electronic failures, a backup system is triggered by an arbitration logic that prioritizes functional safety above all else. To uphold the standards set forth by ISO 26262, rigorous testing of this logic is mandatory. Through this validation, one can confidently ensure the reliability of system responses in times of crisis and prevent aberrant system states from materializing. Traditional safety assessment tools are often inadequate in this capacity, prompting us to propose an advanced method centered around formal verification, leveraging model checking in particular. To demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, we carefully recreate the driving system's dynamics, define and formalize key safety criteria, and scope the analysis within the guidelines specified by ISO 26262. Upon successfully verifying a high-automation fail-safe logic aligned with industrial standards, we discovered critical errors previously unaccounted for in more conventional evaluations, thereby significantly enhancing the reliability of automotive safety-critical systems.

Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by defining a state similarity measure that reflects mutual influence and utilizes the Koopman operator to handle nonlinear relationships, thus extending the approach to a broad spectrum of applications. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through clustering of a linear system, the non-linear 39-bus transmission network, and variables derived from atmospheric data in the Amazon rainforest.

Recent research into Leibnizian calculus has centered on evaluating different fundamental approaches to describe its mathematical processes.  Many scholars, such as Ishiguro and Levey, rely on a Weierstrassian perspective; in contrast, Arthur draws comparisons to the Lawvere-Kock-Bell framework, a non-Archimedean approach known as Smooth Infinitesimal Analysis (SIA). A critical examination of Arthur's comparison reveals significant misunderstandings regarding the nature of the continuous, polygons with an infinite number of sides, and infinitesimal quantities. Additionally, claims by Rabouin and Arthur, suggesting that Leibniz considered infinite quantities to be inherently contradictory, rely on an incorrect blending of Leibnizian concepts of bounded and unbounded infinites - a distinction previously noted by early Knobloch. Instead, a framework developed by Robinson may provide a more accurate account of Leibnizian calculus, which can be formalized using a conservative axiomatic system for infinitesimal analysis called New Mathematical Logic (NML). This formalisation seeks to revive a rigorous approach to mathematical analysis employing infinite quantities, first demonstrated in the late 1960s, which was initially overlooked in favour of the real number architecture due to a preconception of its consistency.

Using the Effective Field Theory of Large Scale Structure, we make predictions for HI intensity mapping power spectrum multipoles based on perturbation theory. These predictions will allow us to constrain cosmological parameters using mildly non-linear scales from data that will be obtained from interferometric HI intensity mapping experiments. Assuming that the experiments will be like CHORD and PUMA, we run a series of analyses on mock data that accurately represents how these surveys are conducted at redshift z=0.5, comparing these to the performance that can be expected from stage 4 optical galaxy surveys. The impact of removing foregrounds using methods that rely on simulations is accounted for in the analysis, which shows how it affects the accuracy of the parameter estimation. The 10 parameters that we vary during the analysis consist of 3 cosmological and 7 non-cosmological parameters. The 4 most relevant parameters are the cold dark matter density, the Hubble constant, the primordial power spectrum amplitude and the linear HI bias. When assuming that foregrounds can be effectively removed, our best case scenario finds that the estimated parameters are accurate with less than a 3% error. When including the impact of foregrounds however, all parameters are estimated inaccurately by more than 5 sigma, indicating that foregrounds removal has to be more accurately handled to avoid biases. Scale cuts, specifically a minimum k-value of about 0.03 h/Mpc, need to be imposed in order to get an accurate estimation of the two

Christensen and Hasannasab established that if a hypothetical operator T transforms sequence vectors $e_n$ into $e_{n+1}$ for all natural numbers, then the sequence is linearly independent only when the dimension of the sequence's vector space is infinite. In our research, we derive this result as a specific instance of a more comprehensive model-theoretic finding. Then, focusing on vector spaces, we demonstrate that if a condition such as $T(e_i)=e_{\phi(i)}$ is to replace the previous operator assumption, $\phi$ must be equivalent to the successor function, defined as incrementing a number by 1. Finally, we explore a more complex generalization of this result, substituting the earlier operator assumption with a more complex condition.

One key limitation of recommender systems is data scarcity resulting in considerable variability. Various approaches have been implemented to optimize the bias-variance equilibrium utilizing supplementary information. In particular, methods incorporating text-based document modeling have significantly improved accuracy by incorporating data like reviews, summaries, and narratives when user-item rating matrices are sparse. Nonetheless, these models are inadequate to learn optimal user and item representations. Collaborative filtering methods, including user-based and item-based, due to their efficiency and clarity, have long been utilized in building recommender systems by generating profiles for each user and item based on their historically interacted items and users. Our research integrates these methods with context-aware document models by taking into account users' perspectives on these items. Additionally, our model offers the advantage of online personalization where the system can adjust the user and item representation profiles upon detecting new user interactions without requiring updates to model parameters. Our proposed method was tested and demonstrated to outperform existing benchmark techniques in reducing variance and achieving better generalization.

Independent unitarily invariant $N\times N$ random matrices exhibit expected asymptotic freeness to $O(N^{-2})$. Infinitesimal freeness in expectation is already known to result from this property. We've established an additional consequence: almost sure asymptotic freeness of type $B$ for unitarily invariant random matrices. This consequence leads to several secondary findings: the asymptotic cyclic monotonicity, and the derivation of asymptotic conditional freeness. Specifically, we demonstrate the empirical spectral distribution of randomly rotated matrices converges towards a conditionally free convolution. We've also identified new relationships between infinitesimal freeness, type $B$ freeness, conditional freeness, cyclic monotonicity, and monotone independence. Moreover, we show that the BBP phase transition in an additive rank-one perturbation of a GUE matrix is a consequence of asymptotic conditional freeness. This line of reasoning applies as well to an analysis of outlier eigenvalues in various unitarily invariant ensembles.

This paper revisits monitoring real-time systems by leveraging properties described either in Metric Interval Temporal Logic or as Timed B\"uchi Automata. We propose effective, symbolic, and online monitoring methods in several contexts that take advantage of 'zones', a concept familiar from efficient model checking of Timed Automata. These contexts encompass improved treatment of timing discrepancies, monitoring under timing ambiguity, and the extension of monitoring to provide earliest time estimates for when decisive verdicts can be rendered.

The decay reactions $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi f_0(980)$ and $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi
a_0(980)$ are examined in detail. Attention is focused on isospin breaking and
the mixing between $f_0(980)$ and $a_0(980)$, both of which are generated by meson-meson interactions. Our analysis indicates that isospin breaking and mixing are primarily responsible for these breakages in isospin symmetry. To further investigate this isospin breaking, a comparison is made with $B^0 \to J/\psi f_0(980)$ and $B^0 \to J/\psi a_0(980)$ and the isospin-breaking factor is evaluated. Our study also shows that the decay width of $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi f_0(980)$ will be smaller than $B^0 \to J/\psi f_0(980)$.

The GRAVITY acquisition camera utilizes four distinct optical capabilities to track multiple beams from the Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI): a) a pupil tracker captures images of reference lasers using a $2 \times 2$ lenslet array, while b) a field tracker captures images of the science target; c) a pupil imager re-images the telescope's pupil, and d) an aberration tracker captures images of a Shack-Hartmann sensor. The camera's detector images are analyzed using dedicated software to determine beam stabilization parameters, every 0.7 seconds. The obtained parameters are then applied to a) adjust the GRAVITY instrument to align with VLTI; b) actively stabilize the telescope's pupil and field of view; c) perform defocus correction, as well as various engineering tasks. The camera has successfully transitioned into operational use, with data reduction and real-time processing techniques having undergone extensive testing and development.

We examine $k$-Center variants in graphs of reduced doubling and highway dimension complexity, specifically the Capacitated $k$-Supplier with Outliers (CkSwO) issue which involves a generalization of traditional $k$-Center with capacity constraints and outlier handling. By understanding the relationship between solution objectives and the highway dimension of the input graph, we demonstrate tight upper and lower bounds for CkSwO approximated schemes with specific parameters. For instance, an efficient CkSwO scheme with specific parameters is possible when the CkSwO instance's solution objective and highway dimension are less than or equal to $k$ and $\alpha$, respectively. Conversely, an NP-hard CkSwO intractability proof exists for instances where the solution objective and highway dimension are both at least $k+1$. Furthermore, this intractability proof also implies the hardness of approximating CkSwO for various general $k$-Center variants and also proves the intractability of approximating CkSwO for certain cases even when the input graph's doubling complexity is known.

In our paper, it's demonstrated that every entire solution of the equation $\Delta_{\eta}^{m}f-Q_1=(\Delta_{\eta}^{k}f-Q_{2})e^{P}$ exhibits hyper-order with the same degree as the polynomial $P$, and based on this result, we establish the differential difference counterpart to Bruck's conjecture. Furthermore, we have also obtained the degree of the hyper-order for solutions of $\Delta_{\eta}^{m}f-Q_1=(\Delta_{\eta}^{k}f-Q_{2})e^{P_{1}}e^{P_{2}}$, which has enabled us to prove Bruck's conjecture itself.

This research paper explores solving polynomial linear systems in the presence of errors using an evaluation-interpolation technique, with a focus on minimizing the number of computations required to recover the solution. This is crucial because it depends on parameters like the degrees and size of the linear system as well as the error rate. As part of an ongoing series on solving polynomial linear systems with errors, we build on our previous findings, including a proof from [Guerrini et al., Proc. ISIT'19], that a lower bound on evaluations can be achieved when errors are randomly distributed, even for large error rates. This paper follows up on [Kaltofen et al., Proc. ISSAC'17] by refining those results in two key ways: introducing a new evaluation bound with reduced dependence on errors, and incorporating an early termination mechanism to prevent unnecessary computations based on conditional probabilities derived from the Berlekamp-Ziberg algorithm.

In the ultrastrong coupling regime of cavity QED, we show that symmetry protects a type of photon bundle emission. The parity symmetry of the Rabi model allows for the creation of super-Rabi oscillations, resulting in the periodic production of even photons in the cavity. This phenomenon is observable through the emission of even photons and is characterized by a long-lived revival time. Following a quantum measurement, the probability of finding the system in the initial state remains high for an extended period, primarily due to the 1/$\sqrt{\epsilon}$ divergence being compensated by a $\sqrt{\epsilon}$-dependent phase factor. Consequently, the decay of these revivals follows a power law, specifically $t^{-3}$, as a result of the exchange of virtual photons, leading to a prolonged period of coexistence between the ground and excited states. This protection of revivals via parity symmetry enables the exploration of novel optical phenomena in systems at the boundary between the Jaynes-Cummings and Molmer-Sorensen regimes.

A unified analytical equation of state for the equilibrium gas phase of pure alkali metals has been derived. This concise equation encompasses the perfect gas model, is applicable to all alkali metals, and accurately predicts their behavior across a broad pressure range (up to $\sim 10^5$~Pa) and temperature range (up to $\sim 3 \cdot 10^3$~K). Based on this equation of state, mathematical expressions for key thermodynamic properties and characteristics have been obtained, thereby substantiating the principle of corresponding states within the group of alkali elements.

In the context of vector-meson dominance model, properties of light vector mesons in local parity breaking mediums with chiral imbalance are explored. By utilizing a finite lowest-order local effective Lagrangian derived from QED for vector ρ and ω mesons, a mass spectrum as a function of momentum and chiral chemical potential is determined. Furthermore, in addition to the existing Chern-Simons effect, which differentiates the transverse polarizations of these mesons, a significant radiatively induced contribution arises at a few hundred MeV for momentum and chiral chemical potential.

We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of the logarithm of the network size, and this estimation is accurate to a large extent (up to 1 - epsilon) among the genuine nodes for any arbitrarily small positive epsilon. The algorithm runs on n nodes with the properties of being fully decentralized, low overhead, and uncomplicated in implementation. Furthermore, the algorithm executes within O(log^3(n)) rounds, necessitates nodes to transmit small data packets in each round, and entails a minimal computation expense per round for each node.

In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian constraint must be resolved.  We demonstrate that this challenge can be overcome when using the Conformal Transverse-Traceless (CTT) metric approach, which enables accurate reconstruction of the metric in scenarios involving symmetry.  A novel, adaptive metric reconstruction technique is proposed, requiring only rough estimates of the metric components as a starting point.  This method is specifically designed for use in simulations of black hole collisions of compact objects, where the Hamiltonian constraint can be solved through a projection operator that ensures consistency with the matter energy-momentum tensor.  By leveraging this technique, we are able to run long-term simulations of black hole collisions with the correct initial conditions, facilitating the study of subsequent phases, including the merger and ringdown.  Our findings for tidal interactions and ringdown frequencies are then compared to those predicted by standard perturbation theory.

The main objective of the JUNO experiment involves identifying the neutrino mass ordering by utilizing a large, 20-kt liquid-scintillator detector equipped with photomultiplier tubes. For optimal results, the experiment's instruments require precise energy resolution and quality, which necessitated a thorough assessment of the PMTs. Over four years, starting from 2017, a rigorous testing program for nearly 20,000 20-inch PMTs was carried out by the JUNO team. By examining these PMTs and implementing a series of stringent requirements, the experiment's investigators were able to verify the high quality of the selected instruments. This study outlines the thorough testing procedures used, the specifically designed testing equipment, and the statistical analysis of the 20-inch PMTs chosen for the experiment, covering over 15 performance indicators, including the uniformity of the photocathode.

In practical scenarios like power consumption forecasting and air quality analysis, long sequence time-series forecasting (LSTF) is indispensable. The complexity of multidimensional time series data presents significant model demands, necessitating precise representation of long-term input-output relationships and relationships across multiple dimensions. Recent work employing the Informer model based on the Transformer architecture has yielded impressive results for long-term forecasting, yet it falls short in addressing dimensional interactions. Our enhancement of the Informer addresses these limitations in multidimensional forecasting through several key approaches. Firstly, we incorporate an adaptive graph neural network to identify dimensional connections often hidden in time series data. Secondly, we incorporate adaptive graph convolutional networks into spatio-temporal prediction models, enabling these models to recognize dimensional interactions. Our empirical evaluations with diverse datasets have revealed that the integration significantly boosts model accuracy by around 10%.

Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes can be distorted by Earth's atmosphere due to differential dispersion that varies by wavelength. Observations made off-axis, other than directly at the zenith, necessitate the use of Atmospheric Dispersion Correctors. Current designs of these correctors are based on atmospheric models which have yet to be verified through on-site measurements. We've carried out a detailed analysis of these models over the 315-665nm wavelength range using cross-dispersion spectrographs, which have an accuracy of 18 milliarcseconds. By comparing various models in detail, we're now in a better position to inform the development of improved ADCs for the future, and advise against relying on the Zemax model, especially when blue spectrum accuracy is critical.

Recently, pre-trained models have significantly impacted ranking systems, delivering outstanding results. To balance high performance with computational efficiency, knowledge distillation is now extensively employed. In this research, we address two critical challenges in knowledge distillation for ranking models: 1) leveraging multiple teachers; and 2) utilizing label data within the distillation process. We introduce the Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE) framework to concurrently address both concerns. By iteratively combining multi-teacher logits guided by label information, PILE has shown superior performance in offline and online experiments. Furthermore, our method has been successfully adapted for online distillation, demonstrating practical value in real-time search and recommendation systems.

Bosonic dark matter, modeled as an ultralight wave-like field near its Compton frequency, can be detectable even when its direct measurement is not sensitive enough to detect the signal directly due to its high frequency, because low-frequency fluctuations will occur below the detection threshold, and can be detected with sensitive instruments that measure variations in pressure or density over extended areas. In our study, we explored the potential for detecting these low-frequency fluctuations using large-scale experiments in physics and related fields. The experiments we considered include atomic interferometry, cold atoms, Rayleigh scattering experiments, and searches for dark matter with large volumes of materials. The potential for detecting ultralight bosonic dark matter signals in these experiments has been evaluated, and the possibility of improving existing setups to increase their sensitivity has been discussed. The improvements that can be made in current setups to increase the sensitivity and detection range have also been identified.

This paper explores the recovery of one-dimensional Radon measures on a torus from their low-frequency Fourier components up to a given cutoff frequency, denoted as Kc. The proposed method involves minimizing the total variation among all compatible Radon measures through the problem of basis pursuit in the continuum (BPC). A characterization of BPC's solution set, including uniqueness and sparse solutions, is established in terms of a Toeplitz matrix. The uniqueness and characteristics of BPC's solution rely on the eigenvalue properties of this matrix. The solutions range from a single, weighted Dirac mass for certain conditions to infinitely many Dirac masses in other cases. The number of Dirac masses in each case is influenced by the rank of a positive or negative semi-definite matrix. The positive or negative definiteness of the matrix also determines the weights of the Dirac masses as either nonnegative or nonpositive, respectively.

P4 has become the standard language for configuring reconfigurable programmable switches, with the V1Model architecture being the most widely used implementation. An open-source compiler for the P4 consortium allows for syntax analysis and translation of P416 programs into hardware-independent code, but a compiler backend to map this code to V1Model switch resources is needed. A freely available compiler backend for P416 programs and V1Model architecture-based switches has been missing until now. Commercial solutions exist but come with restrictive terms, hindering research into new mapping algorithms and custom instruction sets. Our work fills this gap with an open-source compiler backend for the V1Model architecture, utilizing heuristic-based mapping algorithms to optimize P416 programs for different hardware resources. This allows rapid prototyping of different mapping approaches and provides resource usage metrics for comparison. Our source code is publicly available on GitHub for research and development.

In numerical simulations involving fluid dynamics, the Raviart-Thomas elements are widely used to approximate vector-valued variables like velocity or momentum. Nevertheless, the standard finite element methods that employ the lowest-order quadrilateral Raviart-Thomas elements tend to have low spatial accuracy in the vector transport equation. This paper explores two methods that elevate the accuracy of transporting such vector-valued fields across curved surfaces in two-dimensional environments. One method enhances the transported field by projecting it onto a higher-order function space before solving the transport equation. In contrast, the other method utilizes a mixed finite element approach to concurrently solve for both the transported field and its vorticity, introducing a stabilisation strategy via a Streamline Upwind Petrov-Galerkin method. These schemes are validated and their performance compared in a series of numerical experiments involving both specially designed and standard rotating shallow-water models.

The remarkable effectiveness of deep learning has sparked various concerns regarding ethics, encompassing skewed predictions and data security risks. To address these problems, experts employ fairness metrics, decentralized machine learning methods known as federated learning, or differential privacy. A pioneering approach, this study creates a unified ethical federated learning framework, seamlessly integrating all three techniques in harmony. Experimental results based on the Adult, Bank and Dutch datasets showcase the "interplay" between precision, equity, and confidentiality that occurs empirically as a direct outcome.

Scientists analyzed collision data from the LHCb experiment to identify excited states of a particular subatomic particle, known as the B-c plus. They found two peaks in the data, each corresponding to a possible state. One state has a mass of around 6841.2 MeV and fits expectations for a particular state called the second excited B-c plus. The other state has a mass of around 6872.1 MeV and may be consistent with a different state called the B-c plus meson with a superscript plus charge.

In the last few years, the creation of accurate numerical solutions for problems with Hamiltonian dynamics led to the establishment of a specific class of energy-preserving Runge-Kutta methods known as Hamiltonian Boundary Value Methods (HBVMs). These methods can be interpreted as a continuous, multi-step approach, similar to Runge-Kutta methods but with continuous stages, and are explored here in the context of more general differential problems.

This paper introduces an innovative learning method centered on critic networks at a group level, capable of training neural networks using a subset of available data. By dividing the neural network into distinct layer groups and implementing a local critic network for each group, our method facilitates in-depth training of each group using a specific data subset. To maintain consistency between the critic networks and the neural network, we employ a gradient update mechanism for the group parameters. Notably, our method is unique in comparing different group configurations, enabling the identification of layer structures, functionally connected to other layers in the network. To enhance the data efficiency of our method, we introduce an online mean-field reward calculation. Our experimental results demonstrate that our layer group update approach significantly surpasses traditional backpropagation in terms of data efficiency. Moreover, our method exhibits adaptability in handling varying numbers of training examples and is capable of learning neural networks with multiple input and output vectors.

Three-dimensional chaotic scattering has garnered less attention than its two-dimensional counterpart. In this research, a three-dimensional open Hamiltonian system is analyzed where the non-dissipative boundaries initially deviate from Wada's characteristics, changing topologically. Focusing on the effects of dissipation, this study investigates how this system alters when weak dissipation lowers the system's energy below its critical value. Interestingly, this investigation finds that non-Wada basins transition into partially Wada basins under such weak dissipation. Moreover, numerical results demonstrate the emergence of Wada points on the boundaries of these basins in an extensive number. This is consistent with observations in two-dimensional systems. Moreover, this investigation also examines the variation in basin quantities as dissipation decreases and discusses their potential applications in analyzing complex systems.

A theoretical model involving an intricate scalar field that connects to (electron, muon) or (muon, tau) pairs is considered within a certain "duration" window where the mass difference between two lepton types lies between their sum and the absolute difference. In this model, the breaking of lepton level parity could lead to a substantial decay distance between the production and decay points becoming observable. The resulting long-lived particle, resulting from off-shell interactions, may exhibit weakened energy dependence in its cross-section. The proposed particle could be generated through high-energy collisions at the LHC or future CERN projects or possibly detected in naturally occurring cosmic rays.

Human action understanding in complex videos has far-reaching implications, 
which this study addresses by proposing the Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN).
Compared to current deep learning-based methods, HAN stands out due to its
capacity for (1) extended temporal structure capture; (2) explicit modeling of 
temporal transitions between frames and segments, and (3) the ability to learn key 
regions in frames and temporal segments through its multi-step attention mechanism.
Evaluations of the model on established action recognition benchmarks indicate
remarkable performance superiority.

Investigating the thermodynamics and cosmic censorship conjecture in Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes through scalar field scattering yields results that support the first law of thermodynamics for non-extremal black holes, confirming that the singularity in such black holes is hidden by an event horizon. The validity of this theory for near-extremal and extremal black holes is confirmed by analyzing their minimum function values after the scattering process. The findings show that neither near-extremal nor extremal black holes can become overcharged due to such processes. The outcome of scattering when a certain relationship between the electric potential and scalar field is met is that the extremal black hole retains its extreme properties. In contrast, when this relationship is not met, the scattering causes the extremal black hole to transform into a near-extremal black hole with a different mass and charge configuration.

This article will examine the concept of star formation (SF) through observation, and its progression over time, offering a fresh understanding of the process, particularly relevant since planet formation emerges from it and sheds new light on the origins of life in the universe.

This paper proposes a new computational method to evaluate complex probability distributions, specifically by approximating Shannon entropy and mutual information with measurable quantities. Initially, we derive straightforward formulas for evaluating the Shannon entropy of a continuous distribution, effective only in specific circumstances, and conclude that they're not applicable in most cases. Conversely, we find that fractional derivatives effectively calculate the mutual information between two dependent probability distributions, including both continuous and discrete cases. Furthermore, this approach enables the derivation of a fractional time derivative for information flow in dynamic systems, which characterizes the rate at which information changes over time.

We re-examine a widely accepted model for complex semiconductor production lines and analyze it in the context of states, inflows, and outflows being represented by measures on Borel spaces. This investigation arises from the lack of optimal solutions for transitioning from a smaller to a larger equilibrium state with zero inventory levels in the standard L1 framework. Novel contributions involve addressing the issue of non-differentiable velocities with discrete objects and a bounded domain subject to inflows and outflows. Employing a Lagrangian perspective, we establish that solutions exist and are unique and define a notion of weak solutions. Furthermore, we prove that the flow is continuous with respect to time, and also with respect to the initial condition. However, due to generally non-differentiable velocities, these refined regularity results only hold under carefully constructed semi-norms adapted from the standard norm. In general, the solution is not continuous with respect to any standard norm on the space of measures.

Cybersecurity has gained significant importance over recent years, with the detection of cyber threats emerging as a critical task due to the immense damage a single breach can inflict on companies. The incorporation of artificial intelligence (AI) into this task has improved it, allowing high-quality classifiers to detect attacks efficiently; however, these classifiers demand substantial computing power or memory. The scenario presents a problem, particularly when these classifiers need to operate on low-resource devices or prevent performance overload on devices with IoT or industrial applications. A novel solution to overcome this challenge is proposed by NBcoded, a light attack classification tool that effectively combines noisy data removal and efficient data encoding, leveraging the benefits of Naive Bayes classifier while reducing resource requirements. In this study, three NBcoded implementations are developed using three Naive Bayes likelihood distribution assumptions (Gaussian, Complement, and Bernoulli). By comparing the results, NBcoded shows exceptional performance in removing noisy data and achieving high accuracy, making it a reliable choice for classifying cybersecurity threats.

For finitely generated groups G, the focus of this article is the geometric property of growth in graphs representing faithful G-actions. We introduce a concept of Schreier growth gap, a function that measures group growth, by examining its implications on G's set of orbits from finite graphs under group actions. We then show that the existence of non-abelian simple groups within a group or action implies a particular graph theoretical condition, specifically focusing on actions of SL_2(F_p) and showing the existence of Schreier growth gaps in these groups for prime p greater than 5. Moreover, we expand our findings to all finite simple groups, providing evidence of Schreier growth gaps in numerous groups, such as alternating and symmetric groups. Our research reveals connections between group growth, regularity of graphs, and topological properties, shedding light on the complexity of group actions and revealing new aspects of geometric girth in permutation groups.

Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators or mating. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion from raw video footage. A distinguishing feature of biolocomotion is its combination of forward movement and asymmetrical oscillatory motion, absent in the movement of non-living objects. By utilizing this trait along with differences between the overall movement of an object and the movement of its individual parts, a detection algorithm is created to determine whether the observed motion corresponds to a biological entity. Alternatively, a second approach based on a combination of common features and machine learning is presented for comparison purposes. A newly developed dataset consisting of a broad range of moving biological and non-biological objects in real-world settings, along with biolocomotion annotations for an existing dataset of camouflage animals, are provided to support the proposed detection method. Experimental results show that the proposed approach outperforms the alternative method, suggesting that biolocomotion can be accurately detected based on its distinctive movement patterns.

Maximizing efficient electricity usage across transmission power networks requires optimized surplus management to minimize costs.
In our study, we demonstrated the effectiveness of using quantum annealing for optimizing power networks by defining the QUBO problem and implementing solutions on both purely quantum and hybrid architectures.
The D-Wave hybrid solver and classical solvers on Azure Quantum were utilized to solve the problem, yielding hybrid approaches that outperformed classical methods in solution quality or achieved comparable results while reducing computation time.
This innovation marks D-Wave's first entry into the field of power networks and highlights the potential for quantum hybrid algorithms to tackle complex network optimization problems.

Modern artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) methods are now employed to automatically identify physics principles and governing equations directly from measurement data. Nevertheless, formulating a universal physical law using data exclusively proves to be difficult without proposing a corresponding discrepancy model to account for the theoretical framework's shortcomings. By reexamining the long-standing problem of simulating the flow of a Newtonian fluid through a square duct, this work highlights the difficulties of deriving the Navier-Stokes equations from first principles using ML techniques. A thorough evaluation is conducted, comparing the performance of various deep learning algorithms in replicating laminar and transitional flow patterns, as well as their ability to capture underlying physical mechanisms. It is discovered that the ML models used are able to reproduce the Navier-Stokes equations but fail to account for the physical processes driving the observed flow patterns, thereby rendering them ineffective in simulating more complex, turbulent regimes. By investigating this example, this demonstrates that the conventional 'closed-form' approach to deriving universal physical laws may be the most viable methodology for developing robust models, even when supplemented with machine learning techniques.

This study employs the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider to investigate the presence of hypothetical heavy, charged, long-lived particles in proton-proton collisions amounting to 139 inverse femtobarns of data collected at 13 TeV energy. The search targets particles with significantly lower speeds than light and distinctive characteristics: substantial transverse momentum and unusually large energy loss per unit length. The study focuses on particles detectable by their tracks in the inner detector and energy loss measurements in the pixel layers of the detector, thus able to capture particles with lifetimes as short as one nanosecond and masses ranging from 100 GeV to 3 TeV. The study explores the possibilities of long-lived particles in supersymmetric models, considering the production of $R$-hadrons, charginos and staus, with mass limits that extend well beyond previous search findings in various scenarios.

We have developed a numerical approach to maximize coupling efficiency between a single photon and multiple atomic resonances. By optimizing parameters in a finite attenuation model, we achieved a high Purcell factor of 12.9 for individual photons and facilitated the discovery of novel emission patterns at critical points. Consequently, we anticipate significant improvements in the efficiency of single-photon sources utilizing quantum cutting techniques.

Neutron inelastic scattering is a valuable tool that not only allows for the identification of a glass's vibrational modes near its boson peak, but also provides insight into the specific motions involved, thereby facilitating the calculation of dynamic structure factor and sound wave proportions within and below the boson peak, a technique which has been applied to various substances like silicon dioxide, boron oxide, polybutadiene and amorphous germanium. Studies on temperature-dependent boson peaks in silicon dioxide and glycerol have also been conducted. Furthermore, x-ray Brillouin scattering measurements have demonstrated that longitudinal sound wave damping in silicon dioxide and glycerol follows a soft potential model prediction, $\omega^4$, particularly in the low-frequency regime.

Particle physics is becoming a precise science driven by theoretical predictions, 
essential for analyzing experimental data. Future experiments like the LHC 
require advanced computations to understand single-particle behavior and 
production processes. These calculations involve extremely complex equations, 
beyond current analytical methods' capabilities. This study proposes a 
semi-numerical technique using differential equations with specific boundaries 
at unique points to solve these complex equations with high accuracy. These 
calculations can be done using numerical methods like sector decomposition and 
are then translated into physical scenarios with a series solution, providing 
precision of at least eight digits. This method has an integrated accuracy 
checker and is shown to work with challenging examples like self-energy and 
vertex integrals and two-loop box integrals.

In random systems, the scattering matrix correlates incident wave patterns with internal distributions within a volume, and previously this correlation was leveraged to increase energy delivered to a target. This study determines a general set of constraints and formulas governing the eigenvalues and modes within any given scattering setup - including complex geometries, and broad categories such as slabs and narrow channels. Our mathematical framework reveals limitations and correlations for intensity within system boundaries, and derived properties apply universally to different types and strengths of wave, and multiple wave types.

Researchers have identified the far-side counterpart to a well-studied spiral arm in the center of the Milky Way, which is observed expanding. This far-side arm, detected through carbon monoxide emissions, can be followed in a map of Galactic longitude and velocity as a faint feature extending at least 20 degrees. Both the far-side and near-side arms exhibit comparable features including velocities, widths, heights, and mass distribution. Based on further investigation using 21-cm data, it's found that these spiral arms are primarily composed of molecular gas. This new evidence lends support to the presence of a bar structure at the center of the Galaxy and should aid in understanding its properties.

Increasingly, optimization methods are being employed to uncover a broad range of solutions. Our comparison across multi-objective optimization, multimodal optimization, and quality diversity in a straightforward context reveals that multi-objective optimization may not consistently generate significant diversity. By contrast, multimodal optimization tends to yield solutions with superior fitness levels. Meanwhile, quality diversity proves to be resilient to genetic neutrality and yields the most diverse set of solutions overall. Furthermore, integrating an autoencoder allows for the automated discovery of phenotypic features, which, in conjunction with quality diversity, facilitates the creation of a more extensive and diverse solution set. Ultimately, we offer strategic guidance on the appropriate applications of these optimization techniques.

The Stable Roommates problem concerns pairing a set of agents according to their individual preference lists with specific hierarchical rankings. A key condition for any established pairings is that they must remain stable - preventing the situation where two agents would prefer each other over their respective matches. Variants of the Stable Roommates problem, including those involving larger groups of agents and distinct valuation methods, offer alternative scenarios for exploring agent matchings. A more complex form of the Stable Roommates problem, incorporating additively separable valuations and three-dimensional groupings, was explored, revealing instances where no stable matches exist and a direct approach is NP-complete, even when using limited binary valuations. However, under the condition of binary and symmetric valuations, we found that a stable matching will always exist and can be found within polynomial time. Additionally, we looked at finding the best stable matches that maximise total happiness when using binary and symmetric valuations. While finding the absolute optimum is a complex problem, we identified a more practical solution for approximating it closely.

Our research systematically explores how different mechanisms of electron-phonon
interaction affect valley behavior in two-dimensional materials. When we restrict
our study to constant strain conditions, we observe that two mechanisms, cone tilt
and deformation potential, yield analogous effects on valley Hall responses.
However, this equivalence does not apply when we consider dynamic strain effects.
By analyzing a simple and understandable model, we find that both mechanisms
produce distinct valley Hall responses under mobile strain conditions.
Additionally, we investigate the valley Hall effect in the presence of both
spatial and temporal disruptions. Our study offers a comprehensive understanding
of valley behavior in two-dimensional materials when coupled with phonon
interactions, particularly under the influence of strain.

We examine the class of all metric spaces with their distances measured by Gromov--Hausdorff distance. The subsets of spaces with bounded distances are called clouds, representing maximal subclasses within this group. Scaling the distances of a space by a positive factor yields a transformed metric space, belonging to the same Gromov--Hausdorff class. This type of transformation can cause some clouds to jump into others, as noted in our previous study. To explain this phenomenon, we investigated the stability of these space transformations. This paper demonstrates that any cloud having a stabilizer with nontrivial action will contain a unique central metric space, such that transformations from the stabilizer all converge to this space, thereby indicating that it is zero distance away from all others within that group. The key proof for this lies within our previously established cloud completeness theorem.

A microstrip-fed patch antenna designed to operate at mm-waves with broad bandwidth and multiple mode capability has been created. This newly developed antenna has a wide frequency range of 28.1 GHz to 36.3 GHz, giving it a significant bandwidth of 8.2 GHz. When aligned perpendicularly, the antenna exhibits two resonant modes - the primary microstrip patch mode and a coupled patch-fed slot mode. Our research demonstrates that the antenna's characteristics can be replicated in a compact array consisting of four such antennas arranged in a 2x2 pattern.

Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with a code environment, to which reinforcement learning principles can be applied to develop effective decoding tools. Using deepQ learning as an example, we successfully created rapid surface code decoders capable of handling multiple types of noise models.

Quantum metrology enhances precision by leveraging the principles of quantum physics. This can be accomplished through interferometry, by first manipulating highly entangled quantum states before collecting information about an unknown variable through single measurements. Although this typically yields the most effective outcome, applying this method is extremely difficult when dealing with larger states. Another approach is offered by quantum jump metrology, a method that extracts information by continuously monitoring an open quantum system and inducing correlations with the assistance of quantum feedback control. This method is utilised to study the measurement of relative phases in optical systems consisting of two interconnected cavities, and controlled by quantum feedback from laser pulses. The approach is shown to exceed the standard quantum precision limit, without needing highly complex quantum states and with greater scalability and practicality.

The PHENIX Collaboration has collected data from various types of particle interactions, including the collisions of heavy atoms, lighter atoms, and protons. The research aimed to explore how new particles are formed in these interactions and their high-energy properties. In Au+Au collisions, particles carrying a significant portion of their quark's momentum showed a two-fold increase in momentum range compared to p+p collisions. Similarly, particles consisting of two quarks showed both an increase and decrease in momentum range compared to p+p collisions, depending on their multiplicity. These findings suggest the presence of both enhanced and suppressed phenomena in heavy atom collisions. The research also observed altered particle formation patterns and altered high-energy properties in collisions of heavy atoms, lighter atoms, and protons, which can provide insights into the complex phenomena of particle formation and altered high-energy properties in collisions of heavy atoms, lighter atoms, and protons.

In this hybrid digital-analog approach to quantum computing, any quantum algorithm can be implemented without traditional two-qubit gates by utilizing an inherent, always-active quantum connection between qubits. Building on this principle, our research explores how digital-analog simulation can be used to study fermionic systems, specifically the Fermi-Hubbard model, using a fermionic SWAP network and a method to correct distortions. Focusing on the effects of qubit connectivity and the distribution of interaction coefficients, as well as the precision of entanglement-inducing operations, our results indicate that an optimal qubit connectivity arrangement for simulating fermionic systems of any dimensionality is a chain for systems without spin and a ladder for those with spin. This relatively straightforward connectivity arrangement makes the digital-analog method particularly appealing for fermionic quantum simulations.

A common issue in machine learning lies in striking a balance between optimizing performance and robustly handling out-of-distribution (OoD) scenarios. Certain methods rely on complex penalty terms that make the optimization process more resilient to OoD data, but come with no guarantees of improving model generalization. In this research, we introduce a novel approach, called pre-exponential initialization, that provides a solid foundation for the model to thrive in its training environment, thereby enhancing its ability to handle OoD data. This method involves initiating the neural network with a comprehensive representation, thereby accelerating training and reducing the likelihood of model confusion. Our findings using the CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-10 datasets demonstrate that pre-exponential initialization surpasses or competes with state-of-the-art methods in detecting OoD data, while also leading to superior model generalization performance.

Achieving the formation of intricate structures and rapid concentration of light within or through disordered mediums is an arduous endeavor due to variations in refractive index, unpredictable light scattering, and speckle noise generation. To address these challenges, we've developed a novel weighted-mutation-assisted genetic algorithm (WMA-GA) with an R-squared-based fitness function that enhances image clarity, precision, and rapid convergence in forming complex structures within scattering media. As a companion technology to our binary WMA-GA system, we've designed a swift, economical, and reliable iterative wavefront manipulation system that utilizes an affordable ferroelectric liquid crystal (FLC)-based binary-phase spatial light modulator (SLM). This wavefront manipulation system enables the creation of numerous complex 3D heterostructures with an optimized single phase mask. We've verified the efficacy of our proposed approach with 120, 220, 450, and 600 grit ground glass diffusers, as well as with 323, 588, and 852 μm thick fresh chicken tissues including fluorescent properties. We've demonstrated the robustness of our proposed integrated system in controlling photon flow into and out of a localized fluorescent dye embedded in tissue. Detailed results reveal that our algorithm-driven integrated system achieves fast convergence and high image clarity with advanced resolution capabilities.

We appreciate the discussion opportunity facilitated by editors and valuable input from discussants. Our work is influenced by the inspiring research of Kallus (2020), which enhances policy learning efficiency via retargeting. Building upon Dukes and Vansteelandt (2020), we distinguish our research from Kallus (2020) in Section 1 by highlighting their distinct assumptions, variations, and research objectives. In Section 2, guided by Li et al. (2020) and Liang and Zhao (2020), we analyze the efficient policy evaluation problem using data from both the training and testing distributions. Our results demonstrate that under specific growth conditions, efficient value function estimates can yield strong performance, although connections with the representer theorem are minimal due to differing objectives. In Section 3, we emphasize the distinct goals of representer theorem-based analysis and highlight its differences from design of efficient estimates. Our research aims to contribute to the broad area of policy learning, as exemplified by the influential works of Dukes and Vansteelandt (2020) and the comprehensive survey by Zhao (2020).

Monolithic CMOS sensors featuring small collection electrodes are advantageous due to high signal quality and low power consumption. However, these sensors have limited functionality due to the use of thin high-resistivity epitaxial layers during fabrication. In this study, researchers investigate the active sensor depth using the CLICTD technology, a small collection-electrode monolithic demonstrator. Particle beams are utilized to analyze the charge collection properties and device performance across different thicknesses under various beam angles. In CMOS sensors utilizing a high-resistivity Czochralski substrate, a notable enhancement is observed, with the sensitive volume increasing two-fold, subsequently yielding significant gains in detection efficiency and spatial/temporal resolution.

Advanced telescopes strive to spot planets at closer distances, lower masses, or older ages than ever before, with the ultimate goal of directly identifying habitable-zone planets with masses similar to those of Earth. Despite recent technological improvements, a significant barrier remains, with the ability of current high-tech ground-based telescopes limited by image speckles that obstruct our view. This challenge has made it difficult to effectively eliminate the distortions introduced by the atmosphere and the telescope's instruments themselves. To overcome this issue, researchers have proposed a new system known as the Fast Atmospheric Self-coherent camera (FAST), a wavefront sensing and control algorithm that enables the system to operate at the speed of milliseconds even when it detects extremely faint signals. We have successfully tested FAST in the laboratory, showcasing its capability to effectively eliminate the distortions introduced by the atmosphere at the speed of milliseconds.

This study presents a novel exogenous model to tackle the challenge of negative interest rates, maintaining the mathematical ease of the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross model, and accurately replicating the observed yield curve. It combines the difference between two separate Cox-Ingersoll-Ross processes, incorporating the deterministic-shift adjustment, to achieve this goal. To generate the bond prices necessary for Monte Carlo simulations, the research employs a dynamic partial differential equation approach. Multiple numerical techniques are employed, including Euler's method, to examine the bond price trajectories and assess the accuracy of the exogenous model. Furthermore, this study compares the exogenous model with other yield curve models such as the nonlinear G2 model and the extended Tumberg-Svanstedt model.

Research into the characteristics of neutrino oscillations using active neutrinos may also lead to discoveries about sterile neutrinos, specifically in their associated parameters. We investigate the potential of DUNE, a forthcoming experiment, in searching for sterile neutrinos with masses in the GeV range. Our findings rely on the design of DUNE's Near Detector, so we calculated the anticipated sterile neutrino decays within the detector's volume. According to our projections, DUNE may establish a limit comparable to past predictions made for LBNE. We visualize these results for each neutrino type – electron, muon, and tau – indicating that DUNE has a promising capacity to explore previously unexplored areas of sterile neutrino parameter space before the SHiP experiment joins similar research initiatives.

Meta-analyses that include multiple trials based on shared study participants often report correlated effect sizes.  In such scenarios, employing cluster-robust variance estimators can effectively synthesize dependent effects, however these may produce inflated Type 1 errors in cases of a limited number of studies.  In order to improve the performance of robust estimators when dealing with small sample sizes, two new cluster-robust estimators have been developed.  Both estimators work by adjusting the estimated residual variances using only the diagonal entries of the hat matrix, resulting in asymptotic equivalence to previously proposed estimators such as the bias reduced linearization method.  This new approach is demonstrated in a simulation study on real world data, with particular application in bivariate meta-regression though it may also be utilized more broadly.

This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, particle collision, and global updates, and we demonstrate that stretching collision time steps causes inaccuracies in simulations by affecting particle sediment entrainment and the generated turbulence. Our method ensures accurate simulation of complex particle interactions while optimizing computational efficiency.

Investigating the source of radiation energy in the Unruh/Hawking process has shed new light on the particle number definition, particularly as it relates to conservation laws. Research has found that particle radiation is not a product of gravitational force-driven pair creation, but rather an outcome stemming from the disparity in the laws governing particle number definition. In the far distant future, the source of emitted energy corresponds to zero-point fluctuations characterized by exponentially large wave numbers, prompting a reassessment of the black hole evaporation paradigm.

The effect of transverse momentum broadening on parton propagation through a large nucleus is investigated using various models in the color dipole framework. These models generate different values of a key coefficient that influence broadening calculations. Results obtained via numerical analysis are then compared with LHCb and ALICE experimental findings for nuclear broadening in the context of J/Psi particles. Notably, models that align with small-x data are shown to yield transverse momentum variations consistent with measured values, especially in cases where rapidity is in the forward direction. Additionally, model consistency with ALICE measurements is found across various centrality levels.

This article presents $2$ distinct proof methodologies establishing the existence of pairs of relatively prime positive integers, $a$ and $b$, for which the following congruence is satisfied: the expression $a^2+ab+b^2$ can be factored as $7$ raised to a power of $n$.

The video explores the dynamics of a liquid jet that enters a channel filled with the same fluid. As the jet interacts with the surrounding stream, it becomes encircled by a sheath of entrained air. This sheath plays a significant role in the dynamic behavior of the jet and its penetration into the stream. Additionally, we examine the instability effects that develop on the liquid jet and the consequences of these effects on its behavior in the context of fluid dynamics.

High-performance computing systems rely heavily on fault tolerance to prevent data loss and ensure system reliability. Recent advances in non-volatile memory have made it feasible to achieve this, as data in such memory is preserved even during crashes. Nevertheless, the volatility of system caches still poses a significant challenge, as data in these caches can be lost in the event of a crash, necessitating an explicit flush into the main memory to guarantee data integrity. In this study, a new algorithm-based approach is proposed to guarantee data consistency and correctness for high-performance computing applications in systems using non-volatile memory. This method introduces only a minor runtime overhead, allowing developers to leverage the properties of algorithms to verify data integrity after system crashes. Our proposed approach demonstrates significant advantages over traditional checkpointing methods in terms of runtime efficiency while maintaining the ability to correct errors with minimal reprocessing costs. Our comprehensive evaluations, carried out across multiple test scenarios and algorithms such as an iterative solver and dense matrix multiplication, have consistently yielded a remarkably low overhead, at most 8.2 percent in some instances, with most experiments averaging under 3 percent, thereby making this approach an attractive solution for ensuring fault-tolerant HPC applications.

Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content.

We conducted an exhaustive examination comparing the statistical properties of non-hierarchical three-body systems with corresponding theoretical models. By running and analyzing one million simulations for diverse initial conditions, both with and without equal masses in three-body systems, we were able to achieve precise statistical accuracy. Our research focused on escaping trajectories and their distribution of energies, examining how these patterns change with varying masses and DEMs. Our results showed a strong correlation between the theoretical models and our experimental data for a range of DEMs and non-hierarchical systems with equal masses. Notably, our experiments converged with the theoretical predictions of Jensen and Matthieson, specifically obtaining a precise expression for the probability of escape in non-hierarchical systems with equal masses. Our research also explored the influence of DEMs on escaping probabilities and their distribution of energies, finding distinct trends for super-thermal and semi-thermal DEMs. Our comprehensive analysis helped to expand our understanding of statistical dynamics in non-hierarchical three-body systems and their correspondence with theoretical models.

Measurements of the nuclear modification factors of J/$\psi$ and $\psi$(2S) mesons were made in collisions of lead ions at the Large Hadron Collider in 2015. The study was based on data from both lead-lead and proton-proton collisions, involving a total of 5.02 TeV per nucleon pair. The findings show that suppression of both mesons increases with the level of collision centrality, at an extent comparable to that found in previous 2.76 TeV collisions. The study also found that suppression of $\psi$(2S) mesons is stronger than that of J/$\psi$ mesons for each centrality class, indicating a contribution from the dissociation of ground state mesons.

We propose an arrangement of predicates in continuous logic such that the
logical framework's meaning can be structured within a hyperdoctrine framework.
This hyperdoctrine can be incorporated into a hyperdoctrine representing subobjects within a suitable category of topological structures. 
To achieve this incorporation, we first simplify the hyperdoctrine framework for continuous logic and establish an equivalence between its category of equivalence relations and that of complete metric spaces under uniform mappings.

When designing a software system, a modification in one component may
unintentionally impact other parts, hindering overall system performance. This is
addressed by conducting regression testing, which re-evaluates system sections
aimed at preventing adverse effects. However, pinpointing these affected areas
proves challenging, making it essential to identify system changes through a
different approach. We apply singular value decomposition to group software
modifications by their functional roles, allowing for more efficient detection
of areas requiring retesting during subsequent updates. By leveraging parallel
calculations on shared memory systems, we enhance testing speed, ensuring optimal
results can be obtained even as software systems scale up.

A new technique is proposed to forecast suicidal ideation based on the integration of Electronic Health Records and Ecological Momentary Assessment data utilizing advanced deep sequential models. These models leverage clinical information and real-time mental health metrics collected through periodic surveys to predict suicidal ideation. By incorporating varying degrees of clinical information, these models offer adaptable solutions for predicting suicidal ideation with differing levels of complexity and accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly surpasses existing predictive methods in terms of accuracy. Furthermore, an sensitivity analysis reveals that the models are capable of identifying key factors associated with suicidal ideation. These key factors are largely consistent with established psychiatric knowledge, demonstrating the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed method.

Our research reports a significant $\sim 5\sigma$ discovery of polarized X-ray emission within a range of 3-6 keV originating from Cassiopeia A with the IXPE. Our findings reveal a combined polarization level of $1.8 \pm 0.3$%, obtained after summing the polarization vectors from a large region, under the assumption of circular symmetry. Analysis of the synchrotron radiation suggests an average polarization level of $\sim 2.5$%, while the forward shock region indicates a nearly uniform, ordered magnetic field orientation with a limited $3^\circ$ angle of uncertainty. In contrast, the central plateau region displays considerable turbulence in magnetic field orientation with an uncertain magnetic field strength but suggests significant disordered magnetic field components. Our observations of polarization within a limited $3-6$ keV energy range imply considerable Compton backscatter contribution reducing the polarization level by $\sim 50$%. In the forward shock region, our findings indicate a much higher electron energy spectrum index and much higher minimum energy for synchrotron emission compared to previous assumptions, with estimated indices of $\sim 2.2$ and $\sim 10$ keV, respectively. Our polarized X-ray data offers novel insights into the ordered magnetic field component in the forward shock region, while the central region is dominated by chaotic magnetic fields. With its unique properties, our data provides crucial constraints for simulating X-ray emission within a limited frequency range but may

Consider a set $\{a_1, \ldots, a_n\}$ of distinct positive integers where $a_1 < \ldots < a_n$, with the requirement that only subset sums up to a size of at most $\lambda n$ be unique. Erdos originally proposed a conjecture suggesting that $a_n > c \cdot 2^n$, with the current record at $a_n > c \cdot 2^n/\sqrt{n}$. This article presents improved bounds by offering an lower limit of $a_n > c \cdot 2^n/\sqrt{n\log n}$ and demonstrating the uniqueness of subset sums with sizes up to $\lambda n$ for specific values of $\lambda$, specifically $\lambda = 2/\sqrt{\log n}$ or $\lambda = 7/\sqrt{\log n}$ for sufficiently large $n$.

The characteristics of dense matter within the density range of 1-10 times nuclear saturation density, present in compact stars, are intriguingly ambiguous and may influence neutron star dynamics as detected via gravitational waves.
